title: Portable Appliance Testing
subtitle: Five Portable Appliance Testing practice mocks
description: Five Portable Appliance Testing practice mocks covering equipment classes, visual inspection, combined testing, detachable leads, records, limits and practical judgement.
format: Five rotating practice mocks: three 50-question tests, one 30-question test and one 35-question homework paper. Exam format: 80 minutes, open book. Pass at 80%+.

scoring.label: Pass — tighten any missed inspection or limit questions
Near miss — revise Code of Practice fundamentals
Major gaps — rebuild appliance classes, tests and records first

priorities: Equipment classes, protective conductors, insulation and appliance construction.
Formal visual inspection, combined inspection and test, and when each is appropriate.
Earth continuity, insulation resistance, leakage and functional checks.
Detachable leads, surge-protected equipment, extension leads and practical limits.
Record keeping, retest intervals and duty-holder responsibilities.

questions.prompt: Class I equipment:
questions.explanation: Class I equipment relies on basic insulation plus a protective earth connection. The exposed conductive parts must be earthed so a fault current can operate the protective device.

A.text: Class I construction relies on a protective-earth connection to keep accessible conductive parts safe after a basic-insulation fault. Having no earth provision describes a different protective arrangement, not Class I.

B.text: The protective conductor is an essential part of Class I shock protection, not an optional accessory. If that connection is lost, accessible metal could become live without a reliable fault-current path.

C.text: Class I equipment relies on basic insulation plus a protective earth connection. The exposed conductive parts must be earthed so a fault current can operate the protective device.

D.text: This reverses the defining Class I requirement. Class I equipment is designed so its accessible conductive parts are connected to protective earth.

questions.prompt: The most important check, when assessing the level of safety of an electrical appliance, is:
questions.explanation: Visual inspection is the most important check because many dangerous faults are visible before testing. Damaged plugs, cords, cases and misuse are often found this way.

A.text: Earth-leakage testing measures current from live parts to earth or accessible surfaces. It finds leakage, but not visible damage or unsuitable use.

B.text: Flash (hi-pot) testing applies a high voltage to prove dielectric strength. It is not a routine in-service PAT check and can damage insulation or electronics.

C.text: Insulation-resistance testing finds hidden insulation faults. It cannot reveal physical damage or misuse and may be unsuitable for some electronics.

D.text: Visual inspection is the most important check because many dangerous faults are visible before testing. Damaged plugs, cords, cases and misuse are often found this way.

questions.prompt: A flexible cord connected to a 650 W iron should be protected by a fuse rating of:
questions.explanation: A 650 W load at 230 V draws about 2.8 A. The next suitable standard BS 1362 plug fuse is 3 A.

A.text: At 230 V, a 650 W load draws about 2.83 A, so a 2 A fuse is below the appliance's normal current and may operate unnecessarily. The manufacturer's specified fuse rating still takes priority.

B.text: A 650 W load at 230 V draws about 2.8 A. The next suitable standard BS 1362 plug fuse is 3 A.

C.text: Although 4 A exceeds the calculated load current, it is not one of the normal modern replacement ratings. UK appliance guidance generally uses a 3 A or 13 A BS 1362 fuse, with the manufacturer's instruction decisive.

D.text: A 5 A fuse would give the flexible cord less close protection than the 3 A choice that already carries the approximately 2.83 A load. Five-amp fuses remain associated with some older equipment, but are not needed here.

questions.prompt: Equipment users should be competent to inspect:
questions.explanation: Users are expected to spot obvious external defects in accessible equipment and outlets. They should not dismantle equipment, but they can identify damaged or scorched socket outlets.

A.text: Confirming the fuse type and rating may require opening a rewireable plug and belongs to a formal visual inspection by someone trained for that task. A routine user check should remain external.

B.text: The protective conductor is normally inside the flex, plug or equipment, so its integrity cannot be established by a simple user inspection. Where necessary, continuity is verified by a competent person using an appropriate test.

C.text: Users are expected to spot obvious external defects in accessible equipment and outlets. They should not dismantle equipment, but they can identify damaged or scorched socket outlets.

D.text: Terminal security is an internal check and can require opening the plug or equipment. Users should report visible damage rather than dismantle equipment to inspect its terminations.

questions.prompt: Instrument test leads should comply with
questions.explanation: HSE Guidance Note GS 38 sets safety requirements for test leads and probes. It is especially relevant where voltage measurements above extra-low voltage may be made.

A.text: BS 3036 concerns semi-enclosed rewireable fuses, not the construction and safe use of probes and test leads. It provides no requirements for selecting test leads.

B.text: BS 7671 sets requirements for electrical installations. Although test work supports compliance with it, the specific HSE guidance on safe probes, leads, shrouding and current limitation is GS38.

C.text: HSE Guidance Note GS 38 sets safety requirements for test leads and probes. It is especially relevant where voltage measurements above extra-low voltage may be made.

D.text: IET Guidance Note 1 addresses selection and erection of installation equipment; it is not the dedicated guidance for electrical test leads. GS38 is the document named for that purpose.

questions.prompt: When assessing earth continuity of an extension lead under current IET guidance, which limit accounts for the lead conductor's length and cross-sectional area?

options.A: 0.1 Ω plus the calculated protective-conductor resistance R
options.B: 0.1 Ω regardless of the lead length
options.C: Any resistance is acceptable if the lead is shorter than 18 m
options.D: The RCD rating alone determines the continuity limit

questions.explanation: The continuity limit includes the resistance of the lead's protective conductor: 0.1 Ω + R. R is calculated from conductor material, cross-sectional area and length, so a universal maximum length is not the current pass criterion.

A.text: The continuity limit includes the resistance of the lead's protective conductor: 0.1 Ω + R. R is calculated from conductor material, cross-sectional area and length, so a universal maximum length is not the current pass criterion.

B.text: A fixed 0.1 Ω limit ignores the legitimate resistance of the lead's protective conductor. Longer or smaller conductors have more resistance, so the calculated R value must be included.

C.text: Length alone cannot establish satisfactory continuity. The measured result still has to remain within 0.1 Ω plus the calculated protective-conductor resistance.

D.text: An RCD responds to residual-current imbalance; it does not establish the resistance of the lead's protective conductor. Continuity and RCD protection are assessed separately.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct for equipment whose protective-conductor current exceeds 3.5 mA?

options.A: It needs only a label stating the measured current
options.B: Its protective-earthing arrangement must meet the applicable high protective-conductor-current requirements
options.C: A 0.5 mm² protective conductor is always sufficient
options.D: It may be used only in commercial premises

questions.explanation: A protective-conductor current above 3.5 mA requires an appropriately reliable protective-earthing arrangement selected from the applicable product and installation requirements. A label, arbitrary minimum conductor size or workplace type does not by itself control the risk.

A.text: A label communicates information but does not make the protective-earth path sufficiently reliable. The connection arrangement itself must control the shock risk.

B.text: A protective-conductor current above 3.5 mA requires an appropriately reliable protective-earthing arrangement selected from the applicable product and installation requirements. A label, arbitrary minimum conductor size or workplace type does not by itself control the risk.

C.text: A single cross-sectional area cannot be assumed suitable in every case. The conductor and connection method must meet the applicable product and installation requirements.

D.text: The premises type does not make protective-conductor current safe. Suitable protective earthing is required wherever the equipment is installed and used.

questions.prompt: When manufacturer or product-standard information does not specify another value, what maximum protective-conductor current is commonly used for portable or hand-held Class I equipment?
questions.explanation: A commonly used protective-conductor-current limit for portable or hand-held Class I equipment is 0.75 mA. This is a leakage-current criterion, not an insulation-resistance value; the original wording incorrectly mixed the two tests and cited withdrawn BS 3456.

A.text: A 0.5 mA result is below the commonly used 0.75 mA maximum for portable or hand-held Class I equipment. It may be a satisfactory reading, but it is not the stated limit.

B.text: A commonly used protective-conductor-current limit for portable or hand-held Class I equipment is 0.75 mA. This is a leakage-current criterion, not an insulation-resistance value; the original wording incorrectly mixed the two tests and cited withdrawn BS 3456.

C.text: One milliamp exceeds the commonly used 0.75 mA protective-conductor-current limit. The 1.0 MΩ value used in insulation-resistance testing has different units and assesses a different property.

D.text: A 1.25 mA reading is above the 0.75 mA limit. Manufacturer and product-standard information must be followed where it specifies a different criterion.

questions.prompt: Under the current IET Code, how should movement-related descriptions such as 'stationary' and 'portable' affect an equipment maintenance regime?

options.A: They determine a fixed statutory test interval
options.B: Only equipment described as portable needs maintenance
options.C: Equipment over 18 kg is outside the Code
options.D: Movement and handling inform risk but do not by themselves determine the tests

questions.explanation: The current Code removed the former stationary, portable, fixed and moveable categories. How equipment is handled still affects likelihood of damage and therefore risk, but it does not by itself prescribe a test sequence or interval.

A.text: The law does not assign an inspection or test interval from a movement-based category. The dutyholder sets the regime from the equipment's actual risk and maintenance history.

B.text: Electrical equipment can deteriorate and create danger whether it is portable, fixed or seldom moved. Its construction and use determine the necessary maintenance.

C.text: Mass does not remove equipment from electrical-safety management. Heavy equipment still needs suitable inspection, testing and maintenance where risk requires them.

D.text: The current Code removed the former stationary, portable, fixed and moveable categories. How equipment is handled still affects likelihood of damage and therefore risk, but it does not by itself prescribe a test sequence or interval.

questions.prompt: Under current IET guidance, what should determine how often electrical equipment is inspected and, where appropriate, tested?

options.A: Whether it weighs more than 12 kg
options.B: A fixed interval based only on equipment mass
options.C: The next-test date chosen by the tester
options.D: A risk assessment considering environment, users, construction, use and history

questions.explanation: Inspection and test frequency is set by risk assessment, taking account of the environment, users, equipment construction and type, frequency of use, installation method, previous records and expected service life. The former 18 kg category is no longer the basis of the regime.

A.text: Mass alone does not show how likely equipment is to deteriorate or expose a user to danger. Handling, environment, construction and use are also relevant.

B.text: A fixed mass-based interval ignores important differences in users, conditions, frequency of use and previous defects. The interval must reflect the whole risk picture.

C.text: The dutyholder determines the maintenance interval from risk, using competent advice where needed. A tester should not impose the next date independently of that assessment.

D.text: Inspection and test frequency is set by risk assessment, taking account of the environment, users, equipment construction and type, frequency of use, installation method, previous records and expected service life. The former 18 kg category is no longer the basis of the regime.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following would not normally be part of a user inspection:

options.A: Checking security of the flexible cable in its plug top
options.B: Checking the connections within the plug
options.C: Looking for signs of external damage to the equipment
options.D: Operating to check that it works properly

questions.explanation: A user inspection is external and does not normally involve opening the plug. Checking internal plug connections belongs to a formal visual inspection by a competent person.

A.text: A user can look for a flex pulling out of the plug or a failed cord grip without opening the plug. That is an external condition check and should be reported if defective.

B.text: A user inspection is external and does not normally involve opening the plug. Checking internal plug connections belongs to a formal visual inspection by a competent person.

C.text: Looking for cracks, cuts, loose parts, contamination and signs of overheating is central to a user check. These visible defects often reveal danger before an instrument test is considered.

D.text: A normal functional check can form part of safe use, provided no defect is already evident. It does not require dismantling the plug, unlike checking internal terminal connections.

questions.prompt: Class II equipment has an identifying mark in the shape of:

options.C: Two circles, one inside the other
options.D: Two squares, one inside the other

questions.explanation: Class II equipment is identified by the double-square symbol. The mark shows that protection is by double or reinforced insulation, not by an earth connection.

A.text: A single square is not the recognised Class II construction mark. The symbol uses one square inside another to indicate double or reinforced insulation.

B.text: Linked circles are not the Class II symbol and do not communicate double insulation. Equipment classification must be taken from recognised markings and manufacturer information.

C.text: Concentric circles are not the standard mark for Class II equipment. The familiar mark consists of two nested squares.

D.text: Class II equipment is identified by the double-square symbol. The mark shows that protection is by double or reinforced insulation, not by an earth connection.

questions.prompt: New 13A plugs manufactured to BS 1363 will have:
questions.explanation: New BS 1363 plugs have sleeved line and neutral pins. The partial insulation reduces the risk of touching live metal while the plug is being inserted or withdrawn.

A.text: New BS 1363 plugs have sleeved line and neutral pins. The partial insulation reduces the risk of touching live metal while the plug is being inserted or withdrawn.

B.text: The line and neutral pins are only sleeved over part of their length; their contact ends remain conductive so they can engage the socket. Saying simply that the pins are insulated is imprecise and could imply full insulation.

C.text: BS 1363 plug pins are separate line, neutral and earth contacts. They are not interconnected, which would create an electrical fault rather than a safety feature.

D.text: A standard rewireable 13 A plug uses its earth pin for the protective conductor and socket shutters. A plastic shutter-opening pin can appear on some Class II plug-in products, but it is not the defining feature asked about here.

questions.prompt: When conducting an earth continuity test on IT equipment:

options.A: All IT equipment in the area must be disconnected
options.B: Permission should first be sought from the equipment user
options.C: The equipment casing should be removed
options.D: The equipment must be connected to the mains

questions.explanation: Testing IT equipment can interrupt use, risk data loss or affect sensitive electronics. Permission from the user should be obtained before carrying out the earth continuity test.

A.text: Only the equipment and connections affected by the planned test need to be managed. Disconnecting every IT item in the area is unnecessary and may cause avoidable interruption or data loss.

B.text: Testing IT equipment can interrupt use, risk data loss or affect sensitive electronics. Permission from the user should be obtained before carrying out the earth continuity test.

C.text: Routine in-service inspection does not require dismantling the equipment. Removing covers may expose hazards, invalidate approvals or damage the product and should only be done under an appropriate specialist procedure.

D.text: An earth-continuity test uses the protective conductor and an instrument test current; the equipment does not need to be energised from the mains. Connecting it live without the selected procedure would add danger.

questions.prompt: Electrical equipment for use in domestic environments will normally be fitted with a 13A plug manufactured to:
questions.explanation: The normal domestic 13 A plug is made to BS 1363. That standard covers the plug construction and fuse arrangement used in UK homes.

A.text: BS 1362 is the standard for the cartridge fuse-link fitted inside a UK plug, not the construction standard for the plug itself. The two standards work together but cover different components.

B.text: The normal domestic 13 A plug is made to BS 1363. That standard covers the plug construction and fuse arrangement used in UK homes.

C.text: BS 3036 covers semi-enclosed rewireable fuses historically used in installations. It does not specify a domestic 13 A plug.

D.text: BS EN 60898 concerns circuit-breakers for household and similar installations. A circuit-breaker is a distribution protective device, not a plug standard.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the role of an RCD when a long extension lead is used?

options.A: An RCD makes every lead length and load acceptable
options.B: An RCD adds shock protection but does not correct excessive voltage drop, heating or conductor resistance
options.C: A smaller plug fuse removes the need to assess fault protection
options.D: Lead length is irrelevant once the flex is 1.5 mm²

questions.explanation: An RCD can provide additional shock protection, but it does not make an unsuitable lead safe. Load, flex rating, conductor resistance, voltage drop, fault protection, thermal conditions and intended use still require assessment.

A.text: An RCD detects residual current but cannot prevent excessive voltage drop, overload heating or high protective-conductor resistance. The lead and load must still be suitable.

B.text: An RCD can provide additional shock protection, but it does not make an unsuitable lead safe. Load, flex rating, conductor resistance, voltage drop, fault protection, thermal conditions and intended use still require assessment.

C.text: A smaller fuse may limit load current, but fault protection still depends on the complete earth path and disconnection arrangement. Fuse rating alone is not enough.

D.text: Conductor resistance and voltage drop increase with length. Cross-sectional area is important, but it does not make lead length irrelevant.

questions.prompt: Under current general UK consumer guidance, which BS 1362 plug-fuse rating is normally used for an 800 W appliance unless the manufacturer specifies otherwise?
questions.explanation: Current general guidance commonly uses a 13 A plug fuse for appliances rated from about 700 W upward. The appliance manufacturer's specified fuse rating remains decisive; the old keyed 5 A answer reflects superseded multi-rating practice.

A.text: Ten amps is not one of the usual modern replacement ratings in the general 3 A or 13 A consumer guide. The appliance manufacturer's stated rating must be followed where provided.

B.text: Current general guidance commonly uses a 13 A plug fuse for appliances rated from about 700 W upward. The appliance manufacturer's specified fuse rating remains decisive; the old keyed 5 A answer reflects superseded multi-rating practice.

C.text: An 800 W load draws about 3.48 A at 230 V, which is above a 3 A fuse's nominal rating. That fuse could operate during normal use, particularly with starting or heating-current variation.

D.text: Five-amp fuses remain available for some existing equipment, but the current general guide uses 13 A from about 700 W upward. A manufacturer-specified 5 A rating would still take precedence for that product.

questions.prompt: When a standard 13A plug overheats the cause would most likely be due to:

options.A: A loose connection within the plug
options.D: The use of socket outlets not to BS Standards

questions.explanation: A loose terminal creates high resistance at the connection. Under load that resistance produces heat, which is why plugs often overheat at poor connections.

A.text: A loose terminal creates high resistance at the connection. Under load that resistance produces heat, which is why plugs often overheat at poor connections.

B.text: A defective protective-earth connection is a serious shock hazard, but the earth conductor normally carries no load current. It is therefore not the usual cause of a plug heating during ordinary operation.

C.text: A larger conductor has lower resistance and does not inherently produce overheating. Problems arise if a conductor cannot be terminated correctly, but size alone is not the likely cause described.

D.text: A non-compliant or damaged socket could make poor contact, but a loose plug terminal is the direct likely cause of heating within the plug. Its high resistance produces local heat as load current flows.

questions.prompt: The minimum acceptable insulation resistance for Class I heating equipment rated greater than 3 kW is:
questions.explanation: Large heating elements can naturally give lower insulation readings than other Class I equipment. For Class I heating equipment above 3 kW, the minimum accepted value here is 0.3 megohms.

A.text: Large heating elements can naturally give lower insulation readings than other Class I equipment. For Class I heating equipment above 3 kW, the minimum accepted value here is 0.3 megohms.

B.text: A reading of 0.5 MΩ would be above the stated minimum and may pass, but it is not the threshold asked for. The published category value for Class I heating equipment at or above 3 kW is 0.3 MΩ.

C.text: Thirty kilohms is only 0.03 MΩ, one tenth of the stated 0.3 MΩ minimum. That result would not meet the intended insulation criterion.

D.text: Five hundred ohms is 0.0005 MΩ and is far too low for insulation between live parts and accessible earthed metal. It would indicate a potentially dangerous result or an invalid test setup.

questions.prompt: Electrical equipment should be marked with a unique serial number to help:
questions.explanation: A unique serial or asset number links the appliance to its inspection history and records. Without identification, results cannot reliably be tied to the right item.

A.text: A unique serial or asset number links the appliance to its inspection history and records. Without identification, results cannot reliably be tied to the right item.

B.text: A register may record where an item is used, but the number itself identifies the individual asset. Equipment can move while retaining the same unique identifier.

C.text: The identifier links results to the correct asset; it does not perform the test or decide the test method. Test selection depends on construction, manufacturer information, use and risk.

D.text: A serial or asset number does not reveal damage or make the visual inspection more effective. Its role is to make sure observations and results are attributed to the right item.

questions.prompt: Earth continuity testing may sometimes be carried out using:
questions.explanation: A low resistance ohmmeter can verify continuity of the protective conductor where that method is suitable. It measures small resistance values in the earth path.

A.text: A simple bell or buzzer may indicate that some path exists, but it does not provide the accurate low-resistance measurement needed to assess a protective conductor and its terminations.

B.text: A loop-impedance tester is intended for an energised installation loop and is not the normal instrument for measuring an appliance protective-conductor path. Appliance continuity is a low-resistance dead test.

C.text: A low resistance ohmmeter can verify continuity of the protective conductor where that method is suitable. It measures small resistance values in the earth path.

D.text: An insulation tester measures very high resistance between parts that should be separated. Earth continuity requires the opposite type of measurement: a suitably accurate low resistance between the plug earth and accessible earthed parts.

questions.prompt: In the traditional equipment-class system, which class is supplied at separated extra-low voltage and does not rely on protective earthing?
questions.explanation: Traditional Class III equipment is supplied at separated extra-low voltage and does not rely on a protective-earth connection. The original BS 3535 reference is obsolete; modern safety-isolating transformers are covered by the BS EN IEC 61558 series.

A.text: Class 0 equipment relies only on basic insulation and has no protective-earth provision. Its construction is not based on a separated extra-low-voltage supply.

B.text: Class I protection relies on a protective-earth connection so that a fault can operate the protective device. That is different from the extra-low-voltage supply arrangement described.

C.text: Class II equipment relies on double or reinforced insulation and does not need protective earth. It may be supplied at mains voltage and is not defined by the transformer's 50 V output.

D.text: Traditional Class III equipment is supplied at separated extra-low voltage and does not rely on a protective-earth connection. The original BS 3535 reference is obsolete; modern safety-isolating transformers are covered by the BS EN IEC 61558 series.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would not normally form a part of in-service testing:
questions.explanation: Loop testing is a fixed-installation test, not a normal in-service appliance test. PAT focuses on appliance inspection, continuity, insulation/leakage and functional checks.

A.text: Where equipment relies on protective earth, continuity between the earth connection and relevant accessible conductive parts is a core in-service test selected to verify that protection.

B.text: A controlled functional check can help confirm that equipment operates as intended and does not show an obvious unsafe condition. It is part of the overall assessment when appropriate.

C.text: Loop testing is a fixed-installation test, not a normal in-service appliance test. PAT focuses on appliance inspection, continuity, insulation/leakage and functional checks.

D.text: Inspection must precede instrument testing so visible danger, unsuitable equipment or a test that could cause damage is identified first. Testing should never be treated as a substitute for that inspection.

questions.prompt: Electrical equipment users should be:

options.D: Capable of inspecting equipment for obvious defects

questions.explanation: Users are not expected to dismantle equipment or carry out instrument tests. They should be capable of noticing obvious damage or unsafe condition before use.

A.text: Ordinary users are not expected to select instruments, apply electrical tests or interpret readings. Those tasks require additional competence appropriate to the equipment and method.

B.text: A user needs enough instruction to recognise and report obvious danger, but need not possess the broader technical competence required for electrical testing or repair.

C.text: Requiring every equipment user to be an electrician would be disproportionate and is not HSE's maintenance model. Simple user checks can be performed after suitable basic information and training.

D.text: Users are not expected to dismantle equipment or carry out instrument tests. They should be capable of noticing obvious damage or unsafe condition before use.

questions.prompt: Which earth-continuity test approach is preferred by the current IET Code for most Class I equipment?

options.A: A suitable lower-current continuity test, commonly within 20-200 mA
options.C: A 25 A test for every item regardless of construction

questions.explanation: The current Code prefers a suitable lower-current continuity test for most Class I equipment, reducing the risk of damage while still measuring the protective path accurately. A competent person selects the method for the equipment; 25 A is not a universal default.

A.text: The current Code prefers a suitable lower-current continuity test for most Class I equipment, reducing the risk of damage while still measuring the protective path accurately. A competent person selects the method for the equipment; 25 A is not a universal default.

B.text: This is neither the preferred lower-current method nor a correctly timed high-current test. A minute at 13 A could unnecessarily heat the equipment and connections.

C.text: A high current is not suitable as an automatic choice for every item. The test must reflect equipment construction and avoid damaging sensitive protective paths or components.

D.text: Where a high-current method is appropriate, it is normally applied only for a short defined period. One minute is unnecessarily long and is not the preferred routine approach.

questions.prompt: How should the initial user-check frequency be set for a children's ride available to the public in a store entrance?

options.B: From a documented risk assessment, with frequent checks likely because of public use, then revised using findings
options.D: Every six months because the law fixes that interval

questions.explanation: Public handling, vulnerable users, frequency of use and likelihood of damage point toward frequent initial checks, but no single statutory interval applies. The dutyholder sets and reviews the frequency from risk and the defects actually found.

A.text: A universal annual interval ignores frequent public handling and the possibility of damage between checks. A high-use children's ride is likely to need much more frequent observation.

B.text: Public handling, vulnerable users, frequency of use and likelihood of damage point toward frequent initial checks, but no single statutory interval applies. The dutyholder sets and reviews the frequency from risk and the defects actually found.

C.text: One fixed monthly interval cannot account for different usage, environments and defect histories. Findings should be used to shorten or extend the schedule as justified.

D.text: Electrical-safety law does not prescribe a six-month interval for this equipment. The dutyholder must set a suitable frequency from risk.

questions.prompt: Identification of electrical equipment within a duty holder's control is required to produce:
questions.explanation: The duty holder needs to know which items are under control before inspection intervals and records can be managed. Identification feeds directly into the equipment register.

A.text: A fault log records defects after they are found; it is not the primary list created by identifying all equipment under the dutyholder's control. Fault information can be linked to the equipment register.

B.text: A repair schedule deals only with equipment requiring remedial work. Identification first establishes the population of assets that the maintenance system must manage.

C.text: Labels are optional management aids and do not replace a reliable equipment record. HSE does not impose a general legal requirement to label every item that has been checked.

D.text: The duty holder needs to know which items are under control before inspection intervals and records can be managed. Identification feeds directly into the equipment register.

questions.prompt: Which of the following does not apply when testing on a two-core cord set:
questions.explanation: A two-core cord set has no protective conductor. Because there is no earth conductor, an earth continuity test is not applicable.

A.text: A two-core cord set still has line and neutral conductors, so correct end-to-end connection and polarity can be checked where the connector is polarised. The absence of earth does not remove that need.

B.text: Every cord set needs inspection for damage, unsuitable connectors, strain, overheating and exposed conductors. Two-core construction does not make physical defects harmless.

C.text: A two-core cord set has no protective conductor. Because there is no earth conductor, an earth continuity test is not applicable.

D.text: The insulation between the current-carrying conductors and accessible surfaces still needs to be suitable. A two-core lead lacks a protective conductor, but it does not lack insulation.

questions.prompt: Class I equipment with internal electronic components should be tested with a current not greater than:
questions.explanation: Sensitive Class I electronic equipment should not be stressed with a high continuity current. A low-current test not greater than 200 mA reduces the risk of damage.

A.text: Eight hundred milliamps is four times the 200 mA ceiling of the low-current continuity method described for sensitive electronics. It is neither the low-current method nor a conventional high-current bond test.

B.text: Fifteen amps is a high test current and may be unsuitable for sensitive electronic equipment or fine protective-conductor paths. A low-current continuity method is selected to reduce the risk of damage.

C.text: Sensitive Class I electronic equipment should not be stressed with a high continuity current. A low-current test not greater than 200 mA reduces the risk of damage.

D.text: Four hundred milliamps is twice the stated 200 mA maximum for this low-current method. The tester still needs adequate resolution and the result must account for the supply lead's resistance.

questions.prompt: It should be confirmed, when carrying out a formal visual inspection, that electrical equipment is being operated:

options.A: As laid down in the manufacturer's instructions

questions.explanation: Formal visual inspection includes checking that the equipment is suitable and being used correctly. Manufacturer's instructions define the intended operating conditions.

A.text: Formal visual inspection includes checking that the equipment is suitable and being used correctly. Manufacturer's instructions define the intended operating conditions.

B.text: Supply compatibility is important, but voltage alone does not establish correct use. The instructions also cover purpose, loading, environment, ventilation, accessories and other safety conditions.

C.text: Many ordinary appliances are designed for general users and do not require an electrically skilled operator. Any user competence requirement depends on the product and task, as stated by the manufacturer and risk assessment.

D.text: Some equipment may require specific instruction, but that is not a universal condition for all electrical equipment. The broader check is whether actual use follows the manufacturer's instructions.

questions.prompt: When protection against electric shock from equipment is provided using an earth wire, the equipment classification would be:
questions.explanation: If shock protection depends on an earth wire, the appliance is Class I. The protective conductor provides the fault path for exposed metal parts.

A.text: Class 0 construction has only basic insulation and no protective-earth provision. It therefore cannot describe equipment whose fault protection is provided by an earth wire.

B.text: If shock protection depends on an earth wire, the appliance is Class I. The protective conductor provides the fault path for exposed metal parts.

C.text: Class II equipment uses double or reinforced insulation and does not rely on protective earth for safety. The double-square mark, not an earth wire, identifies that construction.

D.text: Class III equipment is associated with an extra-low-voltage supply arrangement and does not use a protective-earth conductor as its basic shock-protection method.

questions.prompt: How should the frequency of user checks for electrical equipment in industrial premises be determined?

options.C: Fortnightly because that interval is statutory
options.D: By risk assessment using environment, use, damage likelihood and maintenance history

questions.explanation: The dutyholder sets the frequency from the actual environment, users, use, likelihood of damage and previous findings. The current IET Code deliberately avoids a fixed industry-category timetable.

A.text: A pre-use check may be justified for equipment exposed to frequent handling or damage, but it is not automatically necessary for every industrial item. The interval must match the risk.

B.text: Daily checks can suit harsh conditions, but applying that frequency to all equipment ignores differences in use, installation and previous findings.

C.text: No statutory fortnightly interval applies. Electrical-safety law requires maintenance sufficient to prevent danger and leaves the dutyholder to determine a suitable regime.

D.text: The dutyholder sets the frequency from the actual environment, users, use, likelihood of damage and previous findings. The current IET Code deliberately avoids a fixed industry-category timetable.

questions.prompt: When conducting insulation resistance tests on new household appliances with Class I insulation, the minimum value would be:
questions.explanation: For new Class I household appliances, the insulation resistance should be at least 1.0 megohm. That shows adequate separation between live parts and accessible earthed metal.

A.text: A quarter of a megohm is below the 1.0 MΩ minimum for this Class I category. A result that low would require investigation rather than acceptance.

B.text: Half a megohm is only half the stated Class I minimum. It should not be confused with current measured in milliamps during a leakage test.

C.text: For new Class I household appliances, the insulation resistance should be at least 1.0 megohm. That shows adequate separation between live parts and accessible earthed metal.

D.text: Two megohms is the commonly stated minimum for Class II equipment. A Class I item may produce a reading above 2 MΩ, but 2 MΩ is not the minimum threshold asked for here.

questions.prompt: Which equipment class is identified by double or reinforced insulation and no reliance on protective earthing?
questions.explanation: Class II equipment uses double or reinforced insulation and does not rely on protective earth. The original wording was non-exclusive because Class 0 and traditional Class III equipment also have no protective-earth provision.

A.text: Class 0 equipment has only basic insulation and no protective-earth provision. It does not provide the double or reinforced insulation that defines Class II construction.

B.text: Class I equipment relies on protective earthing of accessible conductive parts. It is therefore fundamentally different from double-insulated Class II equipment.

C.text: Class II equipment uses double or reinforced insulation and does not rely on protective earth. The original wording was non-exclusive because Class 0 and traditional Class III equipment also have no protective-earth provision.

D.text: Traditional Class III equipment relies on a separated extra-low-voltage supply. Its shock protection is not defined by double or reinforced insulation in the Class II sense.

questions.prompt: According to HSE guidance, what immediate action is required when a user finds faulty electrical equipment?

options.A: Label it but continue using it
options.B: Withdraw it from service but do not report it
options.C: Report it and take it out of use immediately; labelling may help prevent reuse
options.D: Continue using it until the next scheduled test

questions.explanation: The fault should be reported and the equipment taken out of use immediately until competent repair or replacement. A faulty label can help prevent reuse, but HSE presents labelling as a practical control rather than a universal legal requirement.

A.text: A label does not remove the immediate danger while the equipment remains available. Faulty equipment must be taken out of use until it is competently repaired or replaced.

B.text: Withdrawal controls immediate use, but the fault must also be reported so the responsible person can arrange repair, replacement and follow-up.

C.text: The fault should be reported and the equipment taken out of use immediately until competent repair or replacement. A faulty label can help prevent reuse, but HSE presents labelling as a practical control rather than a universal legal requirement.

D.text: Known faulty equipment must not remain in service. Waiting for a scheduled test exposes users to a hazard that has already been identified.

questions.prompt: If a satisfactory-test label is voluntarily used, which information should not be placed on it?

options.A: The date on which the equipment was tested
options.B: A next-test-due date set by the tester
options.C: An indication that the equipment passed satisfactorily
options.D: The asset identifier used by the dutyholder, where applicable

questions.explanation: HSE says an optional label may indicate that equipment passed and when it was tested, but it should not carry a next-test-due date chosen by the tester. The dutyholder decides the next interval from risk assessment.

A.text: The test date records when the satisfactory assessment took place. It can support the dutyholder's maintenance record without prescribing the next interval.

B.text: HSE says an optional label may indicate that equipment passed and when it was tested, but it should not carry a next-test-due date chosen by the tester. The dutyholder decides the next interval from risk assessment.

C.text: Showing that the equipment passed is the principal purpose of a satisfactory-test label. Detailed readings remain in the maintenance record.

D.text: An asset identifier links the label and test record to the correct equipment. It is a useful management control where the dutyholder operates an asset-register system.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the voltage scope of the Electricity at Work Regulations' system-maintenance duty?

options.D: It is not capped at 400 kV; it applies wherever an electrical system may give rise to danger

questions.explanation: Regulation 4 requires systems to be maintained as necessary to prevent danger and states no upper voltage limit. The original 400 kV answer confused a common network voltage with the legal scope.

A.text: The Electricity at Work Regulations do not stop applying at 11 kV. Regulation 4 requires systems to be maintained as necessary to prevent danger and states no upper voltage boundary.

B.text: Although 132 kV is a transmission or distribution voltage, it is not a statutory scope limit in the EWR. The duties are framed around electrical systems, work activity and danger, not this voltage threshold.

C.text: Thirty-three kilovolts is another network voltage, not an EWR scope boundary. Regulation 4 applies its maintenance duty by reference to danger rather than a voltage cut-off.

D.text: Regulation 4 requires systems to be maintained as necessary to prevent danger and states no upper voltage limit. The original 400 kV answer confused a common network voltage with the legal scope.

questions.prompt: Under the current IET Code, how should a fridge freezer be treated for in-service maintenance?

options.A: As portable solely because it has a plug
options.B: According to its construction, installation, use and risk rather than a rigid stationary label
options.C: As moveable solely because it can be repositioned

questions.explanation: The current Code removed rigid stationary, portable, fixed and moveable classifications. A fridge freezer's construction, installation, environment, handling, use and history determine the appropriate maintenance activity.

A.text: A plug does not determine the maintenance regime. Installation, construction, use, handling and environment all affect the risk.

B.text: The current Code removed rigid stationary, portable, fixed and moveable classifications. A fridge freezer's construction, installation, environment, handling, use and history determine the appropriate maintenance activity.

C.text: The ability to reposition equipment does not prescribe its inspection or tests. What matters is how movement and use affect the likelihood of damage.

D.text: A workplace fridge freezer can deteriorate and create shock or fire risk. It must remain within the dutyholder's electrical-safety management arrangements.

questions.prompt: For electrical equipment used on a petrol-station forecourt, which approach is correct?

options.A: Use an ordinary PAT routine without considering the hazardous area
options.B: No maintenance is needed if the equipment is fixed
options.C: Apply office-equipment intervals without further assessment
options.D: Use specialist hazardous-area controls and competent assessment alongside applicable maintenance requirements

questions.explanation: A petrol forecourt presents flammable-atmosphere risks requiring specialist equipment selection, controls and competence. That does not justify a simplistic statement that electrical-equipment maintenance guidance never applies.

A.text: A forecourt can contain a flammable atmosphere, so ordinary appliance procedures alone are insufficient. Equipment, test methods and controls must be suitable for the hazardous area.

B.text: Fixed equipment can deteriorate and ignite a flammable atmosphere. Its installation method does not remove the duty to maintain it safely.

C.text: Office intervals assume a much more benign environment. A forecourt requires a specific hazardous-area assessment by competent people.

D.text: A petrol forecourt presents flammable-atmosphere risks requiring specialist equipment selection, controls and competence. That does not justify a simplistic statement that electrical-equipment maintenance guidance never applies.

questions.prompt: An insulation resistance tester should be capable of:

options.A: Maintaining the test voltage when applied to the equipment insulation
options.B: Supplying a maximum current of 0.5 A through the load
options.C: Supplying a minimum voltage of 1000 V d.c. to the load
options.D: Testing the continuity of a circuit

questions.explanation: An insulation resistance tester must hold the required test voltage while connected to the appliance insulation. Otherwise the reading would not prove the insulation at the specified test stress.

A.text: An insulation resistance tester must hold the required test voltage while connected to the appliance insulation. Otherwise the reading would not prove the insulation at the specified test stress.

B.text: An insulation tester uses a current-limited high-resistance measurement; it is not intended to drive half an ampere through a load. Such a current could be dangerous and would not represent an insulation-resistance test.

C.text: Routine appliance insulation tests commonly offer 250 V or 500 V DC, selected for the equipment. A mandatory minimum of 1000 V could damage modern electronic components and is not a general PAT requirement.

D.text: Continuity is a low-resistance measurement using a different instrument function and test current. An insulation tester establishes that parts intended to be separated have sufficiently high resistance.

questions.prompt: Safety isolating transformers are now covered principally by which standard series?
questions.explanation: The BS EN IEC 61558 series contains the current general and particular safety requirements for transformers and power-supply units. BS 3535 is an obsolete predecessor.

A.text: BS 3526 is not the current safety-isolating-transformer series. It does not establish the applicable separation and transformer safety requirements.

B.text: The BS EN IEC 61558 series contains the current general and particular safety requirements for transformers and power-supply units. BS 3535 is an obsolete predecessor.

C.text: BS 5458 is unrelated to safety-isolating-transformer construction. A standard must be selected by its scope and current status, not numerical similarity.

D.text: BS 5533 does not cover safety isolating transformers. The applicable general and particular requirements are found in the BS EN IEC 61558 family.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes selection of an appliance insulation-resistance test voltage?

options.D: Use 500 V DC where suitable, or a lower-voltage or alternative test where necessary to avoid damage

questions.explanation: Five hundred volts DC is commonly used where the equipment is suitable, but sensitive electronics may require 250 V DC or an appropriate leakage-current method. Test selection must reflect construction and manufacturer information.

A.text: A 1000 V AC dielectric-strength test is not a routine insulation-resistance setting and could damage equipment. In-service insulation resistance is measured with a suitable DC test voltage.

B.text: An insulation-resistance tester applies DC, not a 250 V AC supply. The voltage must also be selected for the equipment rather than applied universally.

C.text: Two hundred and fifty volts DC can protect sensitive electronics, but it is not required for every appliance. Five hundred volts DC is commonly used where the equipment can withstand it.

D.text: Five hundred volts DC is commonly used where the equipment is suitable, but sensitive electronics may require 250 V DC or an appropriate leakage-current method. Test selection must reflect construction and manufacturer information.

questions.prompt: When assessing the level of safety of an electrical appliance the most important check would be:
questions.explanation: Visual inspection is the key safety check because it finds the common real-world defects first. Instrument tests cannot compensate for obvious physical damage or misuse.

A.text: A satisfactory insulation reading addresses only insulation; it does not reveal damaged plugs, leads, enclosures or evidence of misuse.

B.text: Earth-fault current is an electrical characteristic, not a complete appliance-condition check, and it does not reveal visible damage.

C.text: A spot test samples one electrical characteristic and cannot replace a systematic examination of the complete appliance.

D.text: Visual inspection is the key safety check because it finds the common real-world defects first. Instrument tests cannot compensate for obvious physical damage or misuse.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following checks should the user of an appliance be competent to undertake:

options.C: Tests using a portable appliance tester
options.D: Visual inspection of the flexible lead and plug

questions.explanation: A user check should be limited to visible condition, such as the flexible lead and plug. It is intended to catch obvious damage before the appliance is used.

A.text: Ordinary users are expected to make simple external checks, not to choose electrical tests and interpret results. Instrument testing requires additional training and competence.

B.text: A formal visual inspection is systematic and may include opening a rewireable plug, so it is assigned to someone trained and competent for that task. It goes beyond the normal user check.

C.text: Using even a simple pass/fail tester requires instruction in the correct sequence, connections and acceptance criteria. A user cannot be assumed competent to test merely because they operate the appliance.

D.text: A user check should be limited to visible condition, such as the flexible lead and plug. It is intended to catch obvious damage before the appliance is used.

questions.prompt: During a formal visual inspection a check should be made to confirm that the equipment is being operated:
questions.explanation: Formal visual inspection verifies that the appliance is being used as intended. Manufacturer's instructions define safe operation, ventilation, environment and loading.

A.text: Correct supply voltage is only one element of suitability. Instructions can also define intended purpose, duty cycle, ventilation, accessories, environmental limits and required user precautions.

B.text: The necessary user competence depends on the equipment and work; many ordinary products are designed for general users. Safe operation still has to follow the manufacturer information.

C.text: Electrical skill is not a blanket operating requirement for every appliance. Where special skill is necessary, that condition should come from the manufacturer and risk assessment rather than be assumed for all equipment.

D.text: Formal visual inspection verifies that the appliance is being used as intended. Manufacturer's instructions define safe operation, ventilation, environment and loading.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the scope of the current IET Code of Practice for In-service Inspection and Testing of Electrical Equipment?

options.D: It covers workplace electrical equipment broadly, while specialist risks require additional competent controls

questions.explanation: The current Code addresses electrical equipment across a broad range of workplaces. Specialist environments may require extra standards, controls and competence, but 'specialised work situations' is not a meaningful blanket exclusion.

A.text: Hotels are one of many workplace types covered. The Code also addresses offices, shops, industrial premises and other environments where electrical equipment is used.

B.text: Office equipment remains within electrical-safety management even where benign conditions justify less frequent testing. Low risk does not mean exclusion.

C.text: Equipment in shops must be maintained according to its risks, including handling by staff or the public. Specialist controls can supplement rather than remove the Code's guidance.

D.text: The current Code addresses electrical equipment across a broad range of workplaces. Specialist environments may require extra standards, controls and competence, but 'specialised work situations' is not a meaningful blanket exclusion.

questions.prompt: Which regulations contain the specific duty that, where necessary to prevent danger, all electrical systems must be maintained?

options.B: Health and Safety at Work Act 1974
options.C: Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999
options.D: Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998

questions.explanation: Regulation 4(2) of the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 contains the specific system-maintenance duty using this wording. The Health and Safety at Work Act and PUWER impose related duties, which made the original broad question non-exclusive.

A.text: Regulation 4(2) of the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 contains the specific system-maintenance duty using this wording. The Health and Safety at Work Act and PUWER impose related duties, which made the original broad question non-exclusive.

B.text: The Act establishes broad employer duties, including safe plant and systems of work. The specific wording about maintaining all electrical systems where necessary to prevent danger is in EAWR regulation 4(2).

C.text: These Regulations principally require risk assessment and suitable management arrangements. They do not contain the specific electrical-system maintenance duty quoted here.

D.text: PUWER regulation 5 contains a related duty to maintain work equipment efficiently and in good repair. EAWR regulation 4(2) is the source of the specific duty applying to all electrical systems where necessary to prevent danger.

questions.prompt: Which feature should voltage-test probes and leads have under HSE Guidance Note GS38?

options.C: Minimal exposed metal, suitable insulation and appropriate current limitation
options.D: Any construction if the associated tester is used for BS 7671 work

questions.explanation: GS38 calls for probes and leads that minimise exposed metal, are suitably insulated and use shrouding and appropriate current limitation. Those features reduce shock, arcing and short-circuit risk during testing.

A.text: Long exposed tips increase the chance of touching live metal or bridging conductors. GS38 recommends keeping exposed conductive probe material to a minimum.

B.text: Unshrouded connections and a lack of current limitation increase shock and arc risk. Suitable probes use protected connectors and appropriate current-limiting arrangements.

C.text: GS38 calls for probes and leads that minimise exposed metal, are suitably insulated and use shrouding and appropriate current limitation. Those features reduce shock, arcing and short-circuit risk during testing.

D.text: The purpose of the work does not make unsafe leads acceptable. Probe and lead construction must control contact, short-circuit and fault-current hazards.

questions.prompt: How should the formal visual-inspection interval for Class II cleaning equipment used in a school be set?

options.C: From risk assessment and defect history, informed by manufacturer and HSE/IET guidance
options.D: Exactly 6 months because that interval is statutory

questions.explanation: The dutyholder selects an initial interval from the equipment, environment, users and expected damage, then revises it using inspection findings. Current IET guidance does not prescribe the old fixed four-month interval.

A.text: A one-month interval could be justified by severe use or repeated damage, but it is not universally required. Actual conditions and findings must support it.

B.text: A fixed three-month rule ignores differences in equipment, users, cleaning duties and previous defects. The dutyholder must assess those factors.

C.text: The dutyholder selects an initial interval from the equipment, environment, users and expected damage, then revises it using inspection findings. Current IET guidance does not prescribe the old fixed four-month interval.

D.text: Six months may be a reasonable starting point in some circumstances, but it is not a statutory interval. Inspection results should be used to review the frequency.

questions.prompt: If a competent person selects the traditional high-current earth-bond method for a kettle fitted with a 13 A fuse, which test is appropriate?
questions.explanation: For the traditional high-current method, a test current of at least 1.5 times the fuse rating, commonly 25 A for a 13 A fused item, is applied for 5-20 seconds. The method must be suitable for the equipment; the current Code generally prefers a lower-current continuity test.

A.text: Thirteen amps is below the high-current method's minimum of 1.5 times the fuse rating, while a full minute is unnecessarily long.

B.text: Twenty-five amps is suitable for this method, but it should be applied only for the defined 5-20 second period. A minute could cause unnecessary heating or stress.

C.text: For the traditional high-current method, a test current of at least 1.5 times the fuse rating, commonly 25 A for a 13 A fused item, is applied for 5-20 seconds. The method must be suitable for the equipment; the current Code generally prefers a lower-current continuity test.

D.text: Three amps is neither the defined high-current bond value nor a recognised lower-current continuity method. It does not provide the intended test condition.

questions.prompt: Where a supply lead is tested separately, which one of the following is not applicable:

options.A: Earth continuity for a two core supply cord
options.B: Inspection and earth continuity test for a 3 core supply cord

questions.explanation: A two-core supply cord has no protective conductor. With no earth conductor present, an earth continuity test cannot apply.

A.text: A two-core supply cord has no protective conductor. With no earth conductor present, an earth continuity test cannot apply.

B.text: A three-core cord includes a protective conductor, so inspecting it and verifying earth continuity are applicable safety checks rather than the requested exception.

C.text: Insulation and polarity remain relevant to a detachable supply lead. They can reveal damaged insulation or line and neutral conductors connected to the wrong terminals.

D.text: Every cord set needs a visual inspection for damage to its plug, connector, sheath and strain relief, irrespective of whether it contains two or three cores.

questions.prompt: A continuous metal enclosure surrounding Class I equipment, would be classified as:
questions.explanation: A continuous metal enclosure is described as metal-cased. On Class I equipment that metal case is connected to the protective conductor for fault protection.

A.text: “Enclosed” merely says that something has a surrounding case; it does not identify the case material or the Class I protective-earth arrangement described here.

B.text: An insulation-encased item has an insulating outer enclosure. That description conflicts with the continuous metal enclosure stated in the question.

C.text: A continuous metal enclosure is described as metal-cased. On Class I equipment that metal case is connected to the protective conductor for fault protection.

D.text: “Metal insulated” is not the construction descriptor for a continuous metallic outer case. The relevant Class I case is metal and relies on protective earthing.

questions.prompt: If a standard 13 A plug became overheated the probability is that:

options.A: An incorrectly rated cartridge fuse is being used
options.B: Reversed polarity of the phase and earth conductors has occurred
options.D: There is a loose connection at one of the terminals

questions.explanation: Overheating at a 13 A plug is most commonly caused by a loose terminal. The poor connection creates resistance and heat when current flows.

A.text: An unsuitable fuse is a serious defect, but it does not by itself explain local heating at an otherwise normally loaded plug terminal as directly as a resistive loose joint.

B.text: A line-to-earth reversal would create an immediate severe shock hazard and likely operate protection; it is not the usual cause of progressive plug-terminal overheating.

C.text: A poor earth connection compromises fault protection, but the protective conductor normally carries no load current. It is therefore not the usual heat source during normal operation.

D.text: Overheating at a 13 A plug is most commonly caused by a loose terminal. The poor connection creates resistance and heat when current flows.

questions.prompt: The length of a 1.25 mm² extension lead fitted with a standard 13 A plug should not be greater than:
questions.explanation: For a 1.25 mm² extension lead on a standard 13 A plug, the maximum length is 12 m. The limit helps control volt drop and earth fault loop impedance.

A.text: Ten metres is below the cited 12 m recommendation for 1.25 mm² conductors. It can be a safe shorter length, but it is not the maximum asked for.

B.text: For a 1.25 mm² extension lead on a standard 13 A plug, the maximum length is 12 m. The limit helps control volt drop and earth fault loop impedance.

C.text: Fifteen metres is the cited recommendation for the larger 1.5 mm² conductor, not for a 1.25 mm² extension lead with the same plug arrangement.

D.text: Twenty metres exceeds the cited 1.25 mm² recommendation by 8 m, increasing conductor resistance, voltage drop and the resistance of the protective path.

questions.prompt: Ohmmeters which are used to measure the resistance of an earth continuity conductor, must produce a short-circuit current between:
questions.explanation: Low resistance ohmmeters for earth continuity use a small test current. The required short-circuit current range is 20 mA to 200 mA.

A.text: This range starts below the cited lower boundary and stops at only half its upper boundary, so it does not describe the specified low-current continuity range.

B.text: Low resistance ohmmeters for earth continuity use a small test current. The required short-circuit current range is 20 mA to 200 mA.

C.text: Although the lower endpoint is correct, 500 mA is two and a half times the stated 200 mA upper endpoint for this low-current test method.

D.text: Two to ten milliamperes is below the stated range and is not the low-resistance continuity-test current specified by the cited in-service guidance.

questions.prompt: The length of a 1.5 mm² extension lead should not exceed:
questions.explanation: A 1.5 mm² extension lead should not exceed 15 m in this Code of Practice context. Longer leads increase volt drop and fault-loop impedance.

A.text: Twelve metres is the cited maximum for the smaller 1.25 mm² conductor. It is a conservative length for 1.5 mm², but not the requested maximum.

B.text: Fourteen metres remains below the cited 15 m boundary. The question asks for the maximum recommendation, rather than merely a shorter usable length.

C.text: A 1.5 mm² extension lead should not exceed 15 m in this Code of Practice context. Longer leads increase volt drop and fault-loop impedance.

D.text: Twenty-two metres is 7 m beyond the cited recommendation for 1.5 mm² conductors and therefore needs additional design and protective considerations.

questions.prompt: Under current BS 7671, which listed connection method is acceptable for an individual item whose protective-conductor current exceeds 10 mA?

options.A: Permanent wiring, or a BS EN 60309-2 connection with the required protective-conductor arrangement
options.B: Have a label indicating the value of leakage current
options.C: Have protective conductors of not less than 0.5 mm² c.s.a

questions.explanation: Current BS 7671 requires special connection measures for an individual item above 10 mA. Acceptable routes include permanent wiring or a BS EN 60309-2 plug-and-socket arrangement with the specified robust protective conductor; the original BS EN 6030-2 reference was also a typo.

A.text: Current BS 7671 requires special connection measures for an individual item above 10 mA. Acceptable routes include permanent wiring or a BS EN 60309-2 plug-and-socket arrangement with the specified robust protective conductor; the original BS EN 6030-2 reference was also a typo.

B.text: A label can warn about a hazard, but it cannot provide the mechanically reliable protective path required for an item whose normal protective-conductor current exceeds 10 mA.

C.text: A generic 0.5 mm² conductor does not satisfy the current high-protective-conductor-current connection measures, which specify more robust or duplicated arrangements.

D.text: The requirement is governed by protective-conductor current and the connection design, not by describing the premises as an office or another business type.

questions.prompt: Generally speaking, the safety and correct functioning of portable appliances and equipment depends on the integrity of the fixed installation. Requirements for the inspection and testing of fixed installations are given in:
questions.explanation: Portable equipment may depend on the fixed installation for earthing and supply protection. Inspection and testing requirements for fixed installations are covered by BS 7671.

A.text: BS 2001 is not the UK requirements standard governing verification of low-voltage electrical installations, so it is not the fixed-installation reference sought here.

B.text: BS 2754 is not the current wiring requirements for inspecting and testing the supply installation on which Class I equipment may depend.

C.text: Portable equipment may depend on the fixed installation for earthing and supply protection. Inspection and testing requirements for fixed installations are covered by BS 7671.

D.text: BS EN 60898 is a product standard for circuit-breakers. It does not set the overall inspection and testing requirements for a fixed electrical installation.

questions.prompt: What happened to the older 'stationary equipment' category in the 5th edition IET Code of Practice?

options.B: It was removed in favour of assessing the equipment's actual use and risk
options.C: It was renamed Class I equipment

questions.explanation: The 5th edition removed the stationary, portable, fixed and moveable labels. How equipment is actually used can affect risk and maintenance frequency, but an 18 kg threshold no longer determines the inspection and testing regime.

A.text: The 5th edition did not retain the category with a new 15 kg threshold. It removed the stationary and other movement-based category names.

B.text: The 5th edition removed the stationary, portable, fixed and moveable labels. How equipment is actually used can affect risk and maintenance frequency, but an 18 kg threshold no longer determines the inspection and testing regime.

C.text: Class I describes a shock-protection construction that relies on protective earthing. It is not a new name for the former stationary-use category.

D.text: No replacement 25 kg threshold was introduced. Mass and movement can inform risk, but neither creates a current stationary-equipment classification.

questions.prompt: The first test to be applied to an item of Class I equipment is:
questions.explanation: For Class I equipment, the protective conductor must be proven before other electrical tests or energising. Earth continuity is therefore the first electrical test.

A.text: For Class I equipment, the protective conductor must be proven before other electrical tests or energising. Earth continuity is therefore the first electrical test.

B.text: A flash or dielectric-strength test applies a high voltage and is not a routine first in-service test; inappropriate use can overstress insulation and electronics.

C.text: Insulation resistance is selected only after the Class I protective path has been checked. Proving earth continuity first establishes the equipment's primary fault-protection route.

D.text: Polarity is important for cord sets and controls, but it does not first establish continuity from accessible Class I metalwork to the protective-earth contact.

questions.prompt: Which equipment class relies on double or reinforced insulation and therefore does not require a protective-earth connection?
questions.explanation: Class II equipment relies on double or reinforced insulation rather than a protective-earth connection. The original wording was not exclusive because obsolete Class 0 equipment also had no protective-earth provision.

A.text: Class 0 used only basic insulation and lacked a protective earth; it did not provide the double or reinforced insulation that defines the protection asked for.

B.text: Class I equipment relies on a protective-earth connection to accessible conductive parts in addition to basic insulation, which is the opposite of the stated arrangement.

C.text: Class II equipment relies on double or reinforced insulation rather than a protective-earth connection. The original wording was not exclusive because obsolete Class 0 equipment also had no protective-earth provision.

D.text: Class III protection is based on an extra-low-voltage energy source arrangement, not on double or reinforced mains insulation as the defining construction measure.

questions.prompt: Current flowing through a human body when it touches an accessible part is known as:
questions.explanation: Touch current is the current that could pass through a person touching an accessible part. It is the practical leakage current relevant to shock risk.

A.text: Fault current is current caused by an insulation or circuit fault and may flow through a protective conductor; it is not specifically the current through a person touching a part.

B.text: “Shock current” is a descriptive phrase rather than the defined measurement term used for current through a body in contact with an accessible equipment part.

C.text: Supply current is the current drawn by the operating load through its intended circuit. It is not the unintended current that can pass through a touching person.

D.text: Touch current is the current that could pass through a person touching an accessible part. It is the practical leakage current relevant to shock risk.

questions.prompt: Under current IET guidance, why can equipment that is frequently moved require more frequent inspection?

options.A: Its mass automatically changes its shock-protection class
options.B: Movement can increase wear, flexing and mechanical damage
options.C: Every moved item requires a daily instrument test
options.D: Anything below 18 kg is automatically Class II

questions.explanation: The old 18 kg moveable-equipment category was removed. Movement remains relevant because it can increase cable flexing, impact and other damage, which a risk assessment may address with more frequent checks.

A.text: Shock-protection class is determined by equipment construction, such as protective earthing or double insulation, not by the item's mass or how often it moves.

B.text: The old 18 kg moveable-equipment category was removed. Movement remains relevant because it can increase cable flexing, impact and other damage, which a risk assessment may address with more frequent checks.

C.text: Current guidance does not prescribe a universal daily instrument test. The dutyholder selects proportionate checks and tests from the actual risk and experience.

D.text: An item below 18 kg may still be Class I and depend on protective earthing. The former movement threshold never determined its insulation class.

questions.prompt: Which of the following tests assesses compliance with Bs or BS EN Standards:
questions.explanation: Type testing is carried out to prove that a product design complies with the relevant BS or BS EN standard. Routine PAT does not re-type-test the product design.

A.text: In-service inspection and testing assesses whether an individual item remains safe for continued use; it does not re-establish full product-standard design compliance.

B.text: Production tests check manufactured units for specified routine characteristics. They are not the complete assessment of a representative design against every relevant standard requirement.

C.text: Post-repair testing verifies that the repaired item is safe and the repair has not impaired protection; it is not a full product type-conformity programme.

D.text: Type testing is carried out to prove that a product design complies with the relevant BS or BS EN standard. Routine PAT does not re-type-test the product design.

questions.prompt: Damaged equipment must be assessed as to suitability for use by:
questions.explanation: Damaged equipment needs a decision by the responsible person because they control repair, withdrawal or replacement. Users should report damage rather than decide continued use on their own.

A.text: Damaged equipment needs a decision by the responsible person because they control repair, withdrawal or replacement. Users should report damage rather than decide continued use on their own.

B.text: Manufacturer advice may be needed, but the manufacturer does not normally control withdrawal, repair and return-to-service decisions within the user's workplace maintenance system.

C.text: Ownership alone does not establish competence or delegated safety authority. The maintenance system must place the decision with the responsible dutyholder or appointee.

D.text: A user should report the damage and stop using the item, but should not unilaterally decide that damaged equipment is suitable to return to service.

questions.prompt: Low resistance ohmmeters must provide an open-circuit voltage no greater than:
questions.explanation: A low resistance ohmmeter must use a safe open-circuit voltage. The maximum stated value is 24 V.

A.text: Fourteen volts is below the stated ceiling and may fall within an instrument's output, but it is not the maximum open-circuit voltage requested.

B.text: A low resistance ohmmeter must use a safe open-circuit voltage. The maximum stated value is 24 V.

C.text: Forty volts exceeds the specified 24 V ceiling by 16 V and is therefore outside the cited low-resistance ohmmeter test characteristic.

D.text: Four volts is the lower boundary exceeded by the cited Fluke earth-bond output, not the maximum permitted open-circuit value asked for here.

questions.prompt: Which of the following checks/tests does not need to be recorded:
questions.explanation: Satisfactory user checks are informal and normally do not require a written record. Defects found during user checks should still be reported and acted on.

A.text: Although PAT records are not a standalone legal requirement, recording combined inspection and test results is a useful part of monitoring condition, trends and future maintenance decisions.

B.text: A formal visual inspection is a planned maintenance activity. Recording its outcome supports the equipment history and lets the dutyholder review whether the chosen interval is effective.

C.text: Satisfactory user checks are informal and normally do not require a written record. Defects found during user checks should still be reported and acted on.

D.text: A defect found by a user must be reported so the equipment can be taken out of use and controlled until repair; silently treating it as an unrecorded satisfactory check is unsafe.

questions.prompt: No unprotected cables may be run:
questions.explanation: Running unprotected cables under carpets hides damage and can trap heat. It also exposes the cable to crushing and abrasion without being visible.

A.text: A cable visible on a carpet can still create trip and damage risks that must be controlled, but it is not concealed and compressed in the manner singled out here.

B.text: A suitably routed cable on a desk is visible and can be kept clear of sharp edges, heat and strain; its position is not inherently the concealed-damage condition described.

C.text: Running unprotected cables under carpets hides damage and can trap heat. It also exposes the cable to crushing and abrasion without being visible.

D.text: Under-desk routing can be acceptable when the lead is supported and protected from feet, chair mechanisms and sharp edges; the location alone does not prohibit it.

questions.prompt: According to Electrical Safety First's general guide, which statement is correct when selecting a replacement BS 1362 plug fuse?
