options.A: Every appliance should use a 13 A fuse
options.B: Appliances below about 700 W commonly use 3 A, while higher-rated appliances commonly use 13 A
options.C: A 5 A fuse is mandatory for every appliance
options.D: The fuse can be chosen without checking the rating plate or instructions

questions.explanation: The usual modern choices are 3 A and 13 A. Below about 700 W a 3 A fuse is commonly used; from about 700 W upward a 13 A fuse is the general guide, but the manufacturer's specified replacement rating takes precedence.

A.text: A 13 A fuse can be too large to protect the flexible cord of a low-power appliance. The replacement should match the equipment's specified fuse rating.

B.text: The usual modern choices are 3 A and 13 A. Below about 700 W a 3 A fuse is commonly used; from about 700 W upward a 13 A fuse is the general guide, but the manufacturer's specified replacement rating takes precedence.

C.text: Modern appliance plug-fuse selection is generally standardized on 3 A or 13 A. A 5 A fuse may exist in older equipment but is not universally mandatory.

D.text: The rating plate and manufacturer instructions identify the intended load and fuse. Ignoring them can leave the cord inadequately protected or cause unnecessary operation.

questions.prompt: Flexible cables should be inspected for damage:

options.A: At the ends by visual inspection
options.B: At the ends by visual inspection and touch
options.C: Throughout its length by visual inspection
options.D: Throughout its length by visual inspection and touch

questions.explanation: Flexible cable damage can occur anywhere along the lead. Visual inspection and touch along the full length helps find cuts, crushing, kinks and heat damage.

A.text: The plug and appliance entries are common damage points, but limiting the check to those ends can miss cuts, crushing and repairs elsewhere along the lead.

B.text: Adding touch can reveal local deformation at the ends, yet the middle of the flex remains unchecked even though it may have been trapped or abraded.

C.text: A full visual scan is necessary, but careful handling of the disconnected lead can also reveal stiffening, lumps, cuts or crushing that are difficult to see.

D.text: Flexible cable damage can occur anywhere along the lead. Visual inspection and touch along the full length helps find cuts, crushing, kinks and heat damage.

questions.prompt: Under the cited IET extension-lead guidance, the recommended maximum length for a 2.5 mm² extension lead is:
questions.explanation: The cited guidance gives 25 m for 2.5 mm² conductors. This also removes the incomplete wording and exact duplication of the earlier question, which already tests the 15 m recommendation for 1.5 mm².

A.text: Twelve metres is the recommendation associated with 1.25 mm² conductors, so it does not give the cited maximum for the larger 2.5 mm² lead.

B.text: Fifteen metres is the cited value for 1.5 mm² conductors. It is shorter than, and not the specified boundary for, the 2.5 mm² size.

C.text: The cited guidance gives 25 m for 2.5 mm² conductors. This also removes the incomplete wording and exact duplication of the earlier question, which already tests the 15 m recommendation for 1.5 mm².

D.text: Thirty-five metres exceeds the cited 25 m recommendation. A longer lead requires its voltage drop, protective path, load and additional protection to be assessed.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is correct regarding 13A plugs:

options.A: All pins must be partially insulated
options.B: All plugs must have insulated pins
options.C: New plugs must have live pins insulated
options.D: New plugs must have live pins partially insulated

questions.explanation: New BS 1363 plugs must have partially insulated line and neutral pins. The sleeving reduces access to live metal during insertion and removal.

A.text: The earth pin must make the protective connection and operate socket shutters as intended; the partial insulating sleeves apply to the line and neutral pins, not all three pins.

B.text: The conducting ends of plug pins must remain exposed to make electrical contact. The safety feature is partial sleeving of line and neutral, not complete insulation of every pin.

C.text: Fully insulating a current-carrying pin would prevent it making contact. The requirement is partial insulation that leaves the contact end conductive.

D.text: New BS 1363 plugs must have partially insulated line and neutral pins. The sleeving reduces access to live metal during insertion and removal.

questions.prompt: Before disconnecting active IT equipment so that it can be inspected or tested, whose permission should be obtained?

options.B: Permission from the user is required
options.C: The socket circuit must be isolated

questions.explanation: Permission from the user or other person responsible for the active equipment should be obtained before disconnection, because interruption can cause data loss or disrupt work. Manufacturer instructions must also be followed when selecting tests, but that is a separate requirement.

A.text: Manufacturer instructions help select safe test methods, but reading them does not authorize interruption of a user's active work or protect unsaved data.

B.text: Permission from the user or other person responsible for the active equipment should be obtained before disconnection, because interruption can cause data loss or disrupt work. Manufacturer instructions must also be followed when selecting tests, but that is a separate requirement.

C.text: The item should be safely disconnected for dead checks, but isolating the entire socket circuit is not normally required simply to unplug one item after permission is obtained.

D.text: Informing the user is good communication, but the question asks for agreement before disconnection. A notice without permission may still interrupt critical work.

questions.prompt: The maximum protective conductor/touch current allowed for portable hand-held Class I equipment is:
questions.explanation: Portable hand-held Class I equipment has a low touch-current limit because it is held directly by the user. The maximum value stated here is 0.75 mA.

A.text: The cited 0.25 mA figure is associated with Class II accessible-part touch current, not the stated portable or hand-held Class I equipment category.

B.text: Half a milliampere is below the cited 0.75 mA limit. A result below the limit may pass, but it is not the maximum value requested.

C.text: Portable hand-held Class I equipment has a low touch-current limit because it is held directly by the user. The maximum value stated here is 0.75 mA.

D.text: The 3.5 mA figure applies to other Class I equipment in the cited legacy product guidance; hand-held use has the more restrictive 0.75 mA limit.

questions.prompt: For an individual item above 10 mA connected through a 16 A BS EN 60309-2 plug and socket, what minimum protective-conductor cross-sectional area is required in the flexible cable by current BS 7671 guidance?
questions.explanation: For this current BS 7671 connection route, the flexible cable's protective conductor must be at least 2.5 mm² for a 16 A BS EN 60309-2 plug. The original 1.0 mm² value came from superseded equipment guidance.

A.text: Half a square millimetre is only one fifth of the specified minimum and would not provide the enhanced mechanical robustness required for this connection arrangement.

B.text: A 0.75 mm² protective conductor is a common light-flex size, but it is 1.75 mm² below the current requirement for the stated high-current 16 A connection.

C.text: One square millimetre appeared in older product guidance, but current BS 7671 guidance for this 16 A BS EN 60309-2 route specifies at least 2.5 mm².

D.text: For this current BS 7671 connection route, the flexible cable's protective conductor must be at least 2.5 mm² for a 16 A BS EN 60309-2 plug. The original 1.0 mm² value came from superseded equipment guidance.

questions.prompt: A plug connected to equipment with a rating of 1.5 kW should have a fuse rated at:
questions.explanation: A 1.5 kW appliance draws about 6.5 A at 230 V. The suitable standard BS 1362 plug fuse above that load is 13 A.

A.text: A 10 A fuse is above the appliance's normal current, but it is not one of the two preferred replacement ratings in current general consumer guidance for BS 1362 plug fuses.

B.text: A 1.5 kW appliance draws about 6.5 A at 230 V. The suitable standard BS 1362 plug fuse above that load is 13 A.

C.text: At 230 V, a 1.5 kW appliance draws about 6.5 A, so a 5 A fuse is below the normal load current and is liable to operate during ordinary use.

D.text: Seven amperes leaves almost no allowance above the approximate 6.5 A operating current and is not the usual standardized replacement selection for this appliance rating.

questions.prompt: Microwave ovens should be functionally checked to ensure that opening the door:

options.A: Check for leakage of radiation when the door is open
options.B: Check the value of the touch current
options.C: Stops microwave generation through the door interlock
options.D: Ensure the integrity of the insulation resistance

questions.explanation: The safety function is that opening or releasing the door stops microwave generation. It need not remove every electrical supply from the oven, because a display, fan or control circuit may remain powered.

A.text: Operating a microwave with its door open is precisely what the interlock must prevent. A routine PAT sequence should not energize the magnetron in that unsafe condition.

B.text: Touch-current measurement is an electrical safety test, not the functional check that demonstrates the door interlock stops microwave generation when opened.

C.text: The safety function is that opening or releasing the door stops microwave generation. It need not remove every electrical supply from the oven, because a display, fan or control circuit may remain powered.

D.text: Insulation resistance is measured with appropriate test equipment while the appliance is de-energized; opening the door does not itself prove the insulation value.

questions.prompt: An appliance uses supplementary insulation in parts but also relies on a protective-earth connection to accessible conductive parts. How is it classified for in-service inspection?
questions.explanation: Because the protective-earth connection is part of the shock-protection arrangement, the appliance is treated as Class I. The original wording was ambiguous because Class II equipment can have a functional-earth connection that is not a protective earth.

A.text: Class 0 equipment lacks a protective-earth measure and relies only on basic insulation, unlike the stated appliance with an intentional protective-earth connection.

B.text: Because the protective-earth connection is part of the shock-protection arrangement, the appliance is treated as Class I. The original wording was ambiguous because Class II equipment can have a functional-earth connection that is not a protective earth.

C.text: Class II protection must not depend on protective earthing of accessible conductive parts. Supplementary insulation in only part of a product does not remove its Class I reliance.

D.text: Class III equipment relies on an extra-low-voltage source arrangement for protection, not on a mains protective-earth connection to accessible conductive parts.

questions.prompt: Who should determine suitable inspection and test intervals for electrical equipment in a school under current IET guidance?

options.D: The dutyholder, using a risk assessment and competent advice where needed

questions.explanation: The 5th edition removed the old fixed-frequency table. The dutyholder sets and reviews intervals from risk factors such as environment, users, construction, equipment type, use, installation method and previous records.

A.text: The tester can provide competent technical advice, but may not know the school's users, environment, incident history and operational controls well enough to own the interval decision alone.

B.text: Users should make checks and report defects, but an individual user does not control the overall maintenance plan, records or risk assessment for the school's equipment.

C.text: Manufacturer recommendations are an important input, but they cannot account by themselves for the actual environment, frequency of use, damage history and local controls.

D.text: The 5th edition removed the old fixed-frequency table. The dutyholder sets and reviews intervals from risk factors such as environment, users, construction, equipment type, use, installation method and previous records.

questions.prompt: If equipment gives suspect results during an insulation resistance test an alternative test would be a:
questions.explanation: If insulation resistance results are suspect or the test may be unsuitable, a protective conductor or touch-current test can be used instead. It assesses leakage under operating conditions.

A.text: Continuity can verify an earth or conductive path, but it does not measure current leaking from live circuitry to protective earth or an accessible surface under operation.

B.text: Showing that the equipment performs its intended function does not quantify an insulation-related leakage path and therefore cannot resolve a suspect insulation-resistance result.

C.text: If insulation resistance results are suspect or the test may be unsuitable, a protective conductor or touch-current test can be used instead. It assesses leakage under operating conditions.

D.text: An RCD test assesses a residual-current protective device and its operating behavior. It does not determine the appliance's own protective-conductor or touch current.

questions.prompt: If manufacturers test procedures are not available and there is doubt which of the following tests should not be carried out:
questions.explanation: When manufacturer procedures are unavailable and there is doubt, an insulation test should not be applied. The test voltage may damage sensitive components or give misleading results.

A.text: A suitably selected low-current continuity check can verify an accessible protective or functional bond without applying the high DC voltage that creates the concern in this scenario.

B.text: Earth continuity is fundamental where equipment relies on protective earthing, and current guidance prefers a suitable lower-current method rather than omitting the check automatically.

C.text: When manufacturer procedures are unavailable and there is doubt, an insulation test should not be applied. The test voltage may damage sensitive components or give misleading results.

D.text: Polarity of a detachable lead can be checked directly between its plug and connector; it does not require applying a potentially damaging high insulation-test voltage to electronics.

questions.prompt: Why is a bare 'maximum current-carrying capacity' for a 1.5 mm² flexible cable potentially misleading?

options.B: Capacity depends on cable construction, installation, ambient conditions and manufacturer data

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional area alone does not establish one universal current rating. Cable construction, number of loaded cores, ambient temperature, coiling or covering, installation conditions and manufacturer data all affect the permissible current.

A.text: Ten amperes may apply to a particular smaller or differently installed flex, but conductor area alone cannot make it a universal value for every 1.5 mm² cable.

B.text: Cross-sectional area alone does not establish one universal current rating. Cable construction, number of loaded cores, ambient temperature, coiling or covering, installation conditions and manufacturer data all affect the permissible current.

C.text: Twenty amperes could exceed the rating of some 1.5 mm² constructions or installation conditions. A single optimistic number cannot replace the applicable data.

D.text: Six amperes is needlessly restrictive for many 1.5 mm² flexible cables, yet the central error is still claiming one rating without specifying construction and conditions.

questions.prompt: 10 A is equal to:
questions.explanation: One kiloampere is 1000 amperes. Therefore 10 A is 10 / 1000 = 0.01 kA.

A.text: One kiloampere is 1000 amperes. Therefore 10 A is 10 / 1000 = 0.01 kA.

B.text: The prefix kilo represents one thousand, so 0.1 kA equals 100 A. That is ten times the stated current rather than an equivalent expression.

C.text: One ampere is 1,000 mA, making 100,000 mA equal to 100 A. The correct milliampere equivalent of 10 A would be 10,000 mA.

D.text: One thousand milliamperes equals only 1 A. A further factor of ten is needed to represent the stated 10 A current.

questions.prompt: When testing basic insulation the test connection points will be between:
questions.explanation: For a basic insulation test, line and neutral are joined together and tested against earth. That checks insulation between live conductors and accessible earthed parts.

A.text: For a basic insulation test, line and neutral are joined together and tested against earth. That checks insulation between live conductors and accessible earthed parts.

B.text: Testing line to earth alone can leave the neutral-side live circuitry outside the measurement. Linking line and neutral includes both current-carrying paths together.

C.text: Shorting neutral to earth would place one live conductor on the earth side of the measurement and would not form the intended live-conductors-to-earth insulation test.

D.text: A line-to-neutral measurement is across the appliance's normal internal circuit, not between its linked live conductors and the protective or accessible earthed parts.

questions.prompt: Which listed situation is outside the Electricity at Work Regulations because it is not connected with a work activity?

options.A: An employee's own equipment used only for private purposes at home
options.D: Employers equipment used for work at home

questions.explanation: The Regulations apply to electrical systems and equipment in connection with work activities, including employer equipment used for homeworking and employee-owned equipment allowed at work. Purely private domestic use is outside that work-activity scope.

A.text: The Regulations apply to electrical systems and equipment in connection with work activities, including employer equipment used for homeworking and employee-owned equipment allowed at work. Purely private domestic use is outside that work-activity scope.

B.text: Employee ownership does not remove the work connection. If the equipment is permitted and used for work, it can form part of the workplace electrical safety system.

C.text: Employer-provided equipment used in the workplace is a direct example of electrical equipment involved in a work activity and falls within the dutyholder's control.

D.text: Home is the location, but the activity remains work and the employer-provided equipment remains within the work-related electrical safety responsibilities.

questions.prompt: Which of the following should not influence a decision on how often equipment inspection and testing should take place:
questions.explanation: Inspection and test frequency is risk-based, considering use, environment, equipment type and users. Cost should not reduce the frequency needed to control danger.

A.text: Inspection and test frequency is risk-based, considering use, environment, equipment type and users. Cost should not reduce the frequency needed to control danger.

B.text: Wet, dusty, corrosive or mechanically harsh environments can accelerate deterioration, so environment is a core factor when setting a safe inspection interval.

C.text: Hand-held, mobile and fixed equipment experience different handling and fault consequences. The actual equipment type therefore informs the risk-based interval.

D.text: Frequency, duty cycle, movement and foreseeable misuse affect wear and exposure to damage, making actual use directly relevant to the maintenance frequency.

questions.prompt: Under current IET guidance, which earth-continuity approach is generally preferred for routine in-service testing?

options.A: A suitable lower-current continuity test selected for the equipment
options.B: A current equal to the plug-fuse rating
options.C: A mandatory current twice the plug-fuse rating
options.D: A mandatory 26 A test for every item

questions.explanation: The 5th edition gives preference to a suitable lower-current earth-continuity test. The old high-current range was not universally required, and even the former IET source stated a maximum of 25 A rather than 26 A.

A.text: The 5th edition gives preference to a suitable lower-current earth-continuity test. The old high-current range was not universally required, and even the former IET source stated a maximum of 25 A rather than 26 A.

B.text: The fuse rating does not by itself define a suitable test current. Current guidance calls for selecting an appropriate method for the equipment and its circuitry.

C.text: No current rule requiring twice every plug-fuse rating applies to routine in-service testing, and that approach could be unsuitable for sensitive functional-earth paths.

D.text: A universal 26 A test is neither the current preference nor the former documented upper figure, which was 25 A for the older high-current method.

questions.prompt: Training may be required to ensure appliance users are able to carry out:
questions.explanation: Users may need training so they can carry out simple user checks and report defects promptly. That catches obvious faults between formal inspections.

A.text: A formal inspection needs a person with sufficient knowledge and an assigned systematic role. Ordinary user training is aimed at simpler checks and prompt reporting.

B.text: Instrument testing requires additional competence, correct equipment and interpretation of results; it is not an ordinary responsibility created by basic user-check training.

C.text: Users may need training so they can carry out simple user checks and report defects promptly. That catches obvious faults between formal inspections.

D.text: Users should remove defective equipment from use and report it, not open or repair it unless they separately possess the competence and authority for that work.

questions.prompt: If a 0.4 MΩ insulation-resistance result is treated as a purely resistive path, what current does Ohm's law predict at 230 V?
questions.explanation: I = V/R = 230/400,000 = 0.000575 A, or about 0.57 mA. The qualification matters because actual a.c. protective-conductor current can also contain capacitive and electronic-filter components that a d.c. insulation reading does not predict.

A.text: A current of 0.173 mA would correspond to about 1.33 MΩ at 230 V, not the stated 0.4 MΩ resistance used in the calculation.

B.text: I = V/R = 230/400,000 = 0.000575 A, or about 0.57 mA. The qualification matters because actual a.c. protective-conductor current can also contain capacitive and electronic-filter components that a d.c. insulation reading does not predict.

C.text: This result is about thirty thousand times too large. Dividing 230 V by 400,000 Ω produces a fraction of a milliampere, not tens of amperes.

D.text: The numerical digits are close before unit conversion, but 0.000575 A is 0.575 mA, not 575 mA; this option is one thousand times too high.

questions.prompt: Protective conductor currents exceeding 10 mA are unavoidable when using some equipment. In this case special precautions are required. Additional specific information regarding these precautions can be found in:
questions.explanation: Protective conductor currents above 10 mA need special installation precautions. BS 7671 gives the detailed requirements for those protective conductor arrangements.

A.text: Protective conductor currents above 10 mA need special installation precautions. BS 7671 gives the detailed requirements for those protective conductor arrangements.

B.text: The Electricity at Work Regulations impose broad duties to prevent danger, but they do not provide the detailed conductor sizes and connection arrangements requested here.

C.text: IET Guidance Note 1 concerns selection and erection of installation equipment generally; the specific high-protective-conductor-current requirements originate in BS 7671 itself.

D.text: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act establishes general health-and-safety duties. It does not contain detailed electrical connection measures for currents above 10 mA.

questions.prompt: If an appliance has a detachable cord set, a test should be carried out on the appliance

options.C: With the cord set plugged in
options.D: Without the cord set plugged in

questions.explanation: A detachable cord set should be fitted when the appliance is tested so the item is checked as it is used. This also proves the inlet, cord and connections together.

A.text: Probing only the appliance inlet or internal connections bypasses the normal mated cord-and-inlet path, so it does not test the appliance in its assembled supply arrangement.

B.text: The detachable cord also needs its own inspection and test, but that separate check does not replace testing the appliance with a suitable cord connected as used.

C.text: A detachable cord set should be fitted when the appliance is tested so the item is checked as it is used. This also proves the inlet, cord and connections together.

D.text: Without a cord, a plug-connected tester cannot include the appliance inlet and normal supply path. The cord is connected for the appliance test, then tested separately.

questions.prompt: When testing microwave ovens, a check should be made that the warnings concerning microwave energy specified in BS EN 60335-2-25 are:

options.A: Included in the Equipment Instruction Book
options.B: Marked on the relevant covers of the appliance
options.C: Noted in the Equipment Register, Form Va
options.D: Noted on the Equipment Label, Form Vc

questions.explanation: Microwave warning labels must be on the relevant covers so anyone removing them sees the hazard notice. This helps prevent exposure to microwave energy during service or repair.

A.text: Instructions can contain supporting warnings, but a person removing a hazardous cover needs the warning at that cover even when the instruction book is unavailable.

B.text: Microwave warning labels must be on the relevant covers so anyone removing them sees the hazard notice. This helps prevent exposure to microwave energy during service or repair.

C.text: An equipment register supports asset management, but it is not physically present at the point where removing a cover could expose hazardous microwave energy.

D.text: A general inspection label records maintenance status; it is not the product safety marking required on a cover whose removal can expose microwave hazards.

questions.prompt: Where equipment has a protective conductor current designed to exceed 3.5 mA, one requirement is that a label is fixed adjacent to the equipment primary power connection which includes the wording

options.D: CAUTION — HIGH TOUCH CURRENT. Connect to earth before connecting to supply

questions.explanation: The warning must identify the high-touch-current hazard and instruct that the protective-earth connection be made before the supply is connected. 'Warning High Touch Current' alone omits the essential action.

A.text: This phrase identifies a hazard but omits the critical instruction to establish the protective-earth connection before applying the electrical supply.

B.text: “Possibility” understates a designed characteristic and still gives no action for controlling it. The required warning directs the connection sequence explicitly.

C.text: Stating that current is present is incomplete because it does not tell the installer to connect protective earth before the supply, which is the essential precaution.

D.text: The warning must identify the high-touch-current hazard and instruct that the protective-earth connection be made before the supply is connected. 'Warning High Touch Current' alone omits the essential action.

questions.prompt: Class II equipment may be constructed with

options.A: Earthed metalwork separated from live parts by basic insulation only
options.B: Exposed conductive parts connected to the main earthing terminal
options.C: Unearthed metalwork separated from live parts by basic and supplementary insulation
options.D: Unearthed metalwork separated from live parts by basic insulation only

questions.explanation: Class II protection can include unearthed accessible metalwork. It is acceptable only where basic and supplementary insulation separate that metalwork from live parts.

A.text: Basic insulation plus protective earthing is characteristic of a Class I protection arrangement, not Class II double or reinforced insulation independent of earth.

B.text: Relying on an earthing-terminal connection for accessible conductive parts would make protective earth part of the safety measure, contrary to Class II construction.

C.text: Class II protection can include unearthed accessible metalwork. It is acceptable only where basic and supplementary insulation separate that metalwork from live parts.

D.text: With only basic insulation and no protective earth, one insulation failure could make the metal accessible part live. Class II requires an additional or reinforced barrier.

questions.prompt: The term 'equipment construction' relates to

options.A: How the user of equipment is protected against electric shock
options.B: The degree of protection offered against the ingress of moisture or water
options.C: The equipment's suitability for use within specific environmental conditions
options.D: Whether the equipment is hand-held, portable, movable or fixed in use

questions.explanation: Equipment construction describes the method used to protect the user from electric shock. The class of equipment is based on that protective construction.

A.text: Equipment construction describes the method used to protect the user from electric shock. The class of equipment is based on that protective construction.

B.text: Ingress protection is described by an IP classification. It is a separate enclosure property from Class I, II or other shock-protection construction.

C.text: Environmental suitability includes moisture, temperature, impact and contamination ratings; it is broader than the construction class used for electric-shock protection.

D.text: Those are use and movement descriptions, and the 5th edition removed several of the old category labels. They do not define protective construction.

questions.prompt: One purpose of carrying out an earth continuity test, using a low current ohmmeter, on equipment which relies on functional earthing is to ensure that the

options.A: Earthing allows the equipment to operate correctly
options.B: Equipment conforms to the requirements of BS 7822
options.C: Means of isolation from the supply are accessible

questions.explanation: Functional earthing may be needed for screening or correct operation rather than shock protection. The continuity test confirms that functional earth path is present.

A.text: Functional earthing may be needed for screening or correct operation rather than shock protection. The continuity test confirms that functional earth path is present.

B.text: A single continuity measurement cannot demonstrate full conformity with an entire product or installation standard, and BS 7822 is not the governing basis stated here.

C.text: Accessibility of an isolator is established by inspection of its location and operation, not by measuring resistance along a functional-earth conductor.

D.text: A continuity test confirms that a conductive path exists and has low resistance. It does not measure touch current while equipment is energized.

questions.prompt: When conducting an earth continuity test on equipment that has accessible metal parts, which are earthed only for functional/screening purposes, these parts should be

options.A: Subjected to a measured touch current test
options.B: Tested at a current 1.5 times the fuse rating
options.C: Tested at a current between 20 mA to 200 mA
options.D: Tested for earth continuity at full current

questions.explanation: Accessible parts earthed only for functional or screening purposes should be tested gently. A 20 mA to 200 mA test avoids applying a high fault-current test to sensitive circuits.

A.text: Touch-current testing answers a different question about accessible current under operation; it does not replace the requested continuity check of the functional or screening path.

B.text: Scaling the test to the plug fuse is the older high-current approach for protective paths and is unnecessary for metalwork earthed only for function or screening.

C.text: Accessible parts earthed only for functional or screening purposes should be tested gently. A 20 mA to 200 mA test avoids applying a high fault-current test to sensitive circuits.

D.text: A full high-current test can stress or upset sensitive screening circuitry without adding value. A low-current continuity method is appropriate for this non-fault-current path.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a PAT tester's 'soft' earth-continuity test?
questions.explanation: 'Soft' describes the low-current earth-continuity mode used where an unnecessarily high current could be unsuitable. It is not a universal fixed 100 mA value; for example, a current Fluke PAT tester specifies 200 mA for its low-current earth-bond test.

A.text: Dielectric-strength testing applies high voltage across insulation and is unrelated to measuring a low-resistance protective-conductor path with a soft current.

B.text: 'Soft' describes the low-current earth-continuity mode used where an unnecessarily high current could be unsuitable. It is not a universal fixed 100 mA value; for example, a current Fluke PAT tester specifies 200 mA for its low-current earth-bond test.

C.text: Touch current is measured through a specified measuring network on accessible parts, whereas a soft continuity mode injects current through the earth path to measure resistance.

D.text: A functional test checks intended operation, sometimes at supply voltage. It does not establish low-resistance continuity between the earth contact and accessible Class I parts.

questions.prompt: Whilst carrying out an earth continuity measurement on a 3 kW Class I electric fire, the measured resistance slightly increases during the period of test. One possible reason for this increase in resistance could be

options.A: A loose connection at the earth terminal within the mains plug
options.B: An open circuit in the protective conductor
options.C: Degradation of the insulation due to an excessive test current
options.D: Insufficient current supplied by the test equipment

questions.explanation: A resistance that rises during a high-current test suggests heating at a poor connection. A loose earth terminal in the plug is a likely cause.

A.text: A resistance that rises during a high-current test suggests heating at a poor connection. A loose earth terminal in the plug is a likely cause.

B.text: A complete open circuit would produce no valid low-resistance path, normally showing an over-range or fail result rather than a small value that rises gradually.

C.text: The measurement is of the protective conductor, not insulation resistance. Insulation degradation would not normally create a gradual rise in the earth-path resistance reading.

D.text: An unsuitable test current can make a measurement unreliable, but it does not specifically explain a progressive rise as a resistive loose joint heats during the test.

questions.prompt: The main purpose of the cartridge fuse fitted within a standard 13 A plug is to protect the appliance
questions.explanation: The BS 1362 cartridge fuse in a 13 A plug primarily protects the flexible cord set. It disconnects before the cord is damaged by excessive current.

A.text: The BS 1362 cartridge fuse in a 13 A plug primarily protects the flexible cord set. It disconnects before the cord is damaged by excessive current.

B.text: A fuse may prevent cable heating caused by excessive current, but it cannot detect every source of appliance overheating such as blocked ventilation or a failed thermostat.

C.text: Overload is one condition that can operate the fuse, yet the plug fuse is selected primarily so excessive current does not damage the flexible cord supplying the appliance.

D.text: A short circuit can make the fuse operate rapidly, but the appliance still needs its own internal safety design. The plug fuse's principal protected component is the cord set.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is a statutory document?
questions.explanation: The Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 are law and can be enforced. BS 7671 and IET Codes of Practice provide recognised technical standards and guidance, but they are not themselves Acts or Regulations.

A.text: A standard sets an agreed technical benchmark but is not legislation merely because it carries a BS designation. Its use may help demonstrate good practice or compliance with a legal duty.

B.text: The Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 are law and can be enforced. BS 7671 and IET Codes of Practice provide recognised technical standards and guidance, but they are not themselves Acts or Regulations.

C.text: BS 7671 is a national standard for electrical installations rather than an Act or statutory instrument. Legislation may be satisfied by following it, but the publication is not itself law.

D.text: A code provides professional guidance on accepted methods and judgement. It can be persuasive evidence of good practice without acquiring statutory force in its own right.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following regulations states: 'Every employer shall make a suitable and sufficient assessment of the risk to the health and safety of his employees and to persons not in his employment'?

options.C: The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations
options.D: The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations

questions.explanation: That wording is the risk-assessment duty from the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations. It requires employers to assess risks to employees and others affected by the work.

A.text: Supply-quality and distribution requirements do not contain the quoted employer risk-assessment duty. The wording concerns management of workplace health and safety across hazards, not electricity supply alone.

B.text: These impose specific duties concerning electrical systems, work activities and competence. They do not contain the quoted general requirement for a suitable and sufficient employer risk assessment.

C.text: That wording is the risk-assessment duty from the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations. It requires employers to assess risks to employees and others affected by the work.

D.text: PUWER addresses the suitability, maintenance, inspection and safe use of work equipment. Its duties operate alongside, but are not the source of, the quoted general risk-assessment wording.

questions.prompt: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 places relevant duties on:

options.A: Both employees and the general public

questions.explanation: The Act places duties on employers to protect employees and others affected by the work, and duties on employees to take reasonable care and cooperate. It is an Act, not a set of 'Health and Safety at Work Regulations'.

A.text: Employees have express duties, but members of the public are not the other principal workplace dutyholder identified by this pairing. Employers carry the central duties to employees and people affected by the undertaking.

B.text: The Act places duties on employers to protect employees and others affected by the work, and duties on employees to take reasonable care and cooperate. It is an Act, not a set of 'Health and Safety at Work Regulations'.

C.text: Workers must take reasonable care and cooperate, but the Act also imposes extensive duties on employers. Limiting responsibility to workers reverses the structure of workplace safety law.

D.text: Employers carry broad responsibilities, but employees are also required to take reasonable care and cooperate with safety arrangements. Responsibility is therefore not confined to management.

questions.prompt: Which regulations state that, as may be necessary to prevent danger, systems must be maintained so as to prevent such danger so far as is reasonably practicable?

options.C: The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations
options.D: The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations

questions.explanation: This is the maintenance duty in Regulation 4(2) of the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989. It applies where maintenance is necessary to prevent electrical danger.

A.text: This is the maintenance duty in Regulation 4(2) of the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989. It applies where maintenance is necessary to prevent electrical danger.

B.text: BS 7671 contains installation requirements and supports safe maintenance decisions, but it is a non-statutory standard. The quoted legal wording comes from regulation 4(2) of the workplace electrical legislation.

C.text: These require risk assessment and effective management arrangements across workplace hazards. They do not contain the quoted electrical-system maintenance clause.

D.text: PUWER separately requires work equipment to be maintained in an efficient state and good repair. That is a valid parallel duty, but it is not the source of this exact systems-and-danger wording.

questions.prompt: What fixed upper voltage limit does the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 set for its duties?

options.D: No fixed upper voltage limit; the Regulations apply wherever electrical danger may arise

questions.explanation: The Regulations do not stop at 400 kV or any other named voltage. Their duties apply to electrical systems and work activities wherever electrical danger may arise; the precautions needed then depend on the actual risk.

A.text: This is a familiar distribution voltage but not a boundary in the legislation. Higher-voltage systems remain subject to the duties where work activity can give rise to electrical danger.

B.text: Ordinary single-phase utilization voltage is not the top of the statutory scope. The Regulations cover electrical systems at both lower and much higher voltages according to the danger involved.

C.text: A common three-phase utilization voltage does not define the reach of the duties. The legal definitions and requirements are framed around systems, work activities and prevention of danger.

D.text: The Regulations do not stop at 400 kV or any other named voltage. Their duties apply to electrical systems and work activities wherever electrical danger may arise; the precautions needed then depend on the actual risk.

questions.prompt: Which environment requires specialist hazardous-area controls beyond an ordinary in-service electrical-equipment inspection and test routine?
questions.explanation: A petrol-station forecourt may contain flammable vapours, so equipment selection, inspection and work need hazardous-area competence and explosion-risk controls. A normal office-style PAT routine alone cannot manage that ignition risk.

A.text: Electrical equipment at a caravan site still needs maintenance based on use, environment and condition. The location has particular installation requirements, but it is not inherently an explosive-atmosphere workplace.

B.text: Office equipment falls within ordinary electrical safety management even though its environment is often benign. Lower risk may reduce the maintenance frequency; it does not create a hazardous-area inspection regime.

C.text: A petrol-station forecourt may contain flammable vapours, so equipment selection, inspection and work need hazardous-area competence and explosion-risk controls. A normal office-style PAT routine alone cannot manage that ignition risk.

D.text: Retail equipment remains subject to risk-based in-service checks, including items handled by staff or the public. A shop is not automatically classified for flammable vapour hazards.

questions.prompt: The safety and proper functioning of certain portable appliances and equipment depends on the integrity of the fixed installation. Requirements for the inspecting and testing of fixed installations are given in:
questions.explanation: BS 7671 covers verification and periodic inspection of the fixed electrical installation, including its earthing and protective measures. Appliance maintenance does not replace verification of the sockets, circuits and supply that the appliance depends on.

A.text: This is not the current UK requirements standard for low-voltage electrical installations. Selecting an unrelated number would not establish the inspection and testing duties for the supplying wiring.

B.text: BS 7671 covers verification and periodic inspection of the fixed electrical installation, including its earthing and protective measures. Appliance maintenance does not replace verification of the sockets, circuits and supply that the appliance depends on.

C.text: This product standard concerns circuit-breakers for household and similar installations. It does not set the overall verification requirements for the fixed wiring in which those devices are installed.

D.text: This series covers low-voltage switchgear and controlgear products rather than whole-installation inspection and testing. Product compliance cannot replace verification of the complete installation.

questions.prompt: In the traditional movement-based terminology, an electric kettle is classified as:
questions.explanation: A kettle is readily moved from place to place while connected by a flexible cord, so the older terminology called it portable. Current IET guidance focuses on the item's actual construction, use and risk rather than making the label determine the maintenance routine.

A.text: A kettle is a complete freestanding product rather than a component intended to be incorporated permanently into cabinetry or another assembly. It is connected for ordinary use by its detachable base or flexible supply arrangement.

B.text: The user may lift it briefly to pour, but it is not normally held in the hand throughout its energized operation. The traditional hand-held category is aimed at items such as drills or hairdryers used while gripped.

C.text: This older category generally described larger items that could be relocated but were not readily carried in normal use. A domestic kettle is the clearer example of a readily moved plug-connected item.

D.text: A kettle is readily moved from place to place while connected by a flexible cord, so the older terminology called it portable. Current IET guidance focuses on the item's actual construction, use and risk rather than making the label determine the maintenance routine.

questions.prompt: In the traditional movement-based terminology, which domestic appliance would normally be regarded as stationary equipment?
questions.explanation: A washing machine is normally positioned in one place and not moved during operation, so it fits the older stationary category. Current maintenance decisions should still be based on its installation, environment, use and history rather than the category alone.

A.text: This item is commonly secured to the building and supplied as fixed equipment, although the actual product must be checked. That differs from a heavy appliance resting in one operating position.

B.text: Its description expressly says it is incorporated into the building fabric or kitchen unit. The legacy terminology therefore treats it as built-in rather than merely remaining in one place by weight.

C.text: A monitor can normally be relocated without installation work and was historically treated as movable equipment. Its real handling, connections and environment still matter more than the old label.

D.text: A washing machine is normally positioned in one place and not moved during operation, so it fits the older stationary category. Current maintenance decisions should still be based on its installation, environment, use and history rather than the category alone.

questions.prompt: An appliance that relies on the protective conductor in its flexible supply cord for fault protection is classified as:
questions.explanation: Class I equipment uses basic insulation and a protective-earth path. If a live conductor faults to accessible metal, the protective conductor carries fault current so the protective device can disconnect the supply.

A.text: Class I equipment uses basic insulation and a protective-earth path. If a live conductor faults to accessible metal, the protective conductor carries fault current so the protective device can disconnect the supply.

B.text: This construction relies on an appropriately separated extra-low-voltage supply for shock protection. A protective-earth conductor is not its defining safety measure.

C.text: Double or reinforced insulation removes reliance on a protective earth and is identified by the double-square symbol. Its accessible parts remain safe through insulation construction rather than a fault-current path.

D.text: A Class II product may have a metal enclosure, but that metal is separated from live parts by double or reinforced insulation and is not protectively earthed. Metal appearance alone does not make the item Class I.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following arrangements would not meet the protective-conductor requirements in IET guidance?

options.A: Class I equipment supplied by a 1.5 mm² three-core extension lead connected into a 13 A three-pin socket outlet
options.B: Class I equipment supplied by a 2.5 mm² three-core extension lead connected into a BS EN 60309-2 socket outlet
options.C: Class II equipment supplied by a 1.5 mm² two-core extension lead connected into a 13 A three-pin socket outlet
options.D: Class III equipment supplied by a two-core flexible cord connected into the secondary of an isolating transformer supplying SELV lighting equipment

questions.explanation: A BS 1363 extension socket can accept a Class I appliance, so its lead must carry a reliable protective conductor. A two-core lead supplies line and neutral only and would leave subsequently connected Class I metalwork without its required earth path.

A.text: The three-core lead preserves line, neutral and protective-earth continuity to a standard earthed outlet. Its length, conductor rating, fuse and condition must still be suitable for the intended load.

B.text: This arrangement provides the protective conductor on an industrial connector intended for the purpose. Compliance still depends on correct ratings, wiring, environment and inspection condition.

C.text: A BS 1363 extension socket can accept a Class I appliance, so its lead must carry a reliable protective conductor. A two-core lead supplies line and neutral only and would leave subsequently connected Class I metalwork without its required earth path.

D.text: A two-core connection is consistent with equipment whose shock protection is provided by the appropriately separated extra-low-voltage source. It does not require a protective conductor in the utilization circuit.

questions.prompt: Which listed test is inherently inapplicable to Class II equipment because it has no protective conductor to verify?

options.A: Earth continuity test on Class II equipment
options.B: Earth continuity tests (for Class I equipment)

questions.explanation: Class II equipment does not rely on a protective conductor, so there is no Class II earth path to prove with an earth-continuity test. Its enclosure, double or reinforced insulation and any suitable insulation or touch-current test are assessed instead.

A.text: Class II equipment does not rely on a protective conductor, so there is no Class II earth path to prove with an earth-continuity test. Its enclosure, double or reinforced insulation and any suitable insulation or touch-current test are assessed instead.

B.text: Where safety relies on protective earth, the path from the supply earth to accessible conductive parts must be verified by an appropriate low-resistance method. Inspection alone cannot quantify that connection.

C.text: An insulation or suitable alternative leakage assessment is selected where needed to verify separation from hazardous live parts. The exact method and voltage must suit the equipment and manufacturer information.

D.text: Visual examination is essential before applying instrument tests because it can reveal damage, unsuitable use or a test that might cause harm. A satisfactory meter result cannot override an obvious defect.

questions.prompt: Which activity would normally generate a formal appliance inspection-and-test record?

options.D: User check revealing no damage to equipment

questions.explanation: A combined inspection and test produces a formal result that the dutyholder can link to the asset, findings and maintenance history. A satisfactory informal user check does not normally need an individual test record.

A.text: Relevant standards may be cited in a procedure, but a list of publications is not itself an equipment maintenance event. The useful record identifies the asset, activity, outcome and any action required.

B.text: A combined inspection and test produces a formal result that the dutyholder can link to the asset, findings and maintenance history. A satisfactory informal user check does not normally need an individual test record.

C.text: Maker details can assist identification or technical enquiries but do not record the condition found on a particular date. An asset register does not substitute for documenting a completed formal assessment.

D.text: HSE says records are not normally needed for the simplest satisfactory pre-use checks. Users should promptly report a defect, while formal inspections and tests provide more useful auditable maintenance evidence.

questions.prompt: Which approach should not be used by itself to set an appliance inspection-and-test interval?

options.A: Environment in which it is to be used
options.C: A blanket annual interval applied regardless of risk

questions.explanation: There is no universal legal rule that every appliance must be tested annually. Intervals come from risk: how and where the item is used, who uses it, its construction, likelihood of damage and what previous checks found.

A.text: Moisture, dust, heat, vibration and mechanical abuse affect how quickly equipment may become unsafe. An arduous setting therefore forms a central part of the frequency risk assessment.

B.text: Construction affects the protective measures on which safety depends; for example, Class I relies on an earth connection while Class II relies on insulation. That difference informs what to check and how often.

C.text: There is no universal legal rule that every appliance must be tested annually. Intervals come from risk: how and where the item is used, who uses it, its construction, likelihood of damage and what previous checks found.

D.text: Training, care, reporting behaviour and the likelihood of misuse all change the chance that damage will go unnoticed. User characteristics are consequently a recognised risk factor.

questions.prompt: How should the initial user-check frequency for a children's ride at a fairground be selected?

options.B: From a site-specific risk assessment, with frequent checks likely and the interval reviewed from findings

questions.explanation: Public use, vulnerable users, movement, weather and rough handling can justify checks before opening or at another frequent interval. The dutyholder must set and review that interval from the actual risk; 'daily' is not a universal statutory figure.

A.text: A fixed annual check ignores intensive public use, outdoor exposure, transport and assembly damage. The interval could be far too long unless an evidence-based assessment demonstrated otherwise.

B.text: Public use, vulnerable users, movement, weather and rough handling can justify checks before opening or at another frequent interval. The dutyholder must set and review that interval from the actual risk; 'daily' is not a universal statutory figure.

C.text: A monthly schedule might form one part of a justified maintenance plan, but it cannot be prescribed from the equipment name alone. Actual use, environment and defect history must support the choice.

D.text: Weekly checks may be appropriate in some operating conditions, yet this remains an unsupported calendar answer without the site's evidence. Findings and changes in use should shorten or extend the interval as necessary.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following tests should not be applied routinely to equipment:
questions.explanation: Dielectric strength testing applies a high stress voltage and can damage insulation if used unnecessarily. It is not a routine in-service PAT test.

A.text: Dielectric strength testing applies a high stress voltage and can damage insulation if used unnecessarily. It is not a routine in-service PAT test.

B.text: Protective-conductor verification is an ordinary selected test for Class I items and extension leads. A suitable low current is now preferred where it can reliably assess the accessible earth path.

C.text: This is a normal option when the equipment and its electronics can tolerate the chosen DC voltage. A lower voltage or leakage-current alternative may be required for vulnerable modern products.

D.text: Conductor assignment is appropriately checked on extension leads, detachable cord sets and rewireable connections. That verification does not impose the high insulation stress associated with a flash test.

questions.prompt: The first electrical test to be applied to Class I equipment is:
questions.explanation: For Class I equipment, the earth path must be proven before other electrical tests. Earth continuity confirms exposed metalwork can clear a fault safely.

A.text: A high-voltage strength test is not a routine first in-service measurement and may damage equipment. Visual examination and the protective-earth path take priority for this construction.

B.text: For Class I equipment, the earth path must be proven before other electrical tests. Earth continuity confirms exposed metalwork can clear a fault safely.

C.text: Insulation is important, but the defining Class I fault-protection path should be established first. The test voltage and any alternative method must then be selected for the actual equipment.

D.text: Conductor assignment is checked where applicable to plugs, leads and controls, but it does not precede verification of the accessible protective-earth path. The latter is fundamental to Class I safety.

questions.prompt: If an optional inspection-and-test label is used, which information belongs in the full maintenance record rather than on the label?

options.A: An indication of whether the equipment has passed or failed the safety tests

questions.explanation: The item's previous readings and findings belong in its maintenance record, where trends can be reviewed. A simple voluntary label may identify the item and show the outcome and test date, but it is not a substitute for the record.

A.text: Current status is the label's most immediate safety information under the stated scheme. It helps users distinguish an accepted item from one identified as unsafe or awaiting action.

B.text: An asset identifier connects the physical item to the correct register entry and measured results. Without it, identical products can easily be confused after relocation.

C.text: The completed-test date provides useful evidence of when the labelled status was established. It should not be confused with prescribing an automatic next-test date independently of risk.

D.text: The item's previous readings and findings belong in its maintenance record, where trends can be reviewed. A simple voluntary label may identify the item and show the outcome and test date, but it is not a substitute for the record.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is outside the equipment-maintenance scope of the IET Code of Practice because it is covered by installation verification requirements?
questions.explanation: The fixed wiring installation is verified and periodically inspected under BS 7671. The IET equipment Code addresses electrical equipment used in service; it does not turn an appliance inspection into an EICR of the supplying installation.

A.text: Tools used at work can be heavily handled and exposed to mechanical damage, making risk-based inspection particularly important. Their supply arrangement and construction determine any selected tests.

B.text: The current Code deliberately includes equipment wired into the installation, such as air-conditioning or access-control units. Being secured in place does not move the equipment into the installation wiring standard's scope entirely.

C.text: The fixed wiring installation is verified and periodically inspected under BS 7671. The IET equipment Code addresses electrical equipment used in service; it does not turn an appliance inspection into an EICR of the supplying installation.

D.text: Plug-connected and readily moved products remain part of in-service electrical safety management. The current Code uses the broader word equipment without excluding these familiar items.

questions.prompt: What does HSE's Memorandum of Guidance on the Electricity at Work Regulations advise about equipment records?

options.A: Are not required if the equipment is fed from a 110 V safety supply
options.B: Are not required where the equipment is used in low-risk areas
options.C: Only be kept where the equipment is used in high-risk areas
options.D: Should be kept throughout the working life of the equipment

questions.explanation: Keeping records throughout the equipment's working life gives the dutyholder evidence of faults, repairs, deterioration and maintenance decisions. Records are strongly useful evidence of an effective system even though the Regulations do not prescribe one universal PAT record format.

A.text: A reduced-voltage supply can lower shock risk but does not prevent flex damage, earth faults, overheating or misuse. It provides no general exemption from a useful maintenance history.

B.text: A benign environment may justify less frequent activity, but records still help demonstrate and review that judgement. Low risk changes the maintenance plan rather than erasing its evidence.

C.text: The guidance does not restrict record value to arduous workplaces. Results and fault history help a dutyholder adjust intervals and understand deterioration wherever the item is used.

D.text: Keeping records throughout the equipment's working life gives the dutyholder evidence of faults, repairs, deterioration and maintenance decisions. Records are strongly useful evidence of an effective system even though the Regulations do not prescribe one universal PAT record format.

questions.prompt: The person responsible for carrying out an inspection and test on an appliance should have made available to them:

options.A: A copy of the Electricity at Work Regulations
options.B: A copy of the Health and Safety at Work Act
options.C: A list of all the users of the equipment

questions.explanation: Previous results let the inspector compare readings, spot deterioration or recurring damage and judge whether the maintenance regime is effective. A list of every person who used the item does not provide that technical history.

A.text: The competent person should understand the relevant legal duties, but a copy of the statutory instrument does not describe this asset's condition or history. It cannot reveal a deteriorating trend.

B.text: General legislation provides context for workplace responsibilities rather than item-specific evidence. The inspector needs information that can be compared with today's observations and readings.

C.text: Patterns of use can inform risk assessment, but every individual's name is unnecessary for performing the equipment check. The asset's prior findings provide the directly relevant comparison baseline.

D.text: Previous results let the inspector compare readings, spot deterioration or recurring damage and judge whether the maintenance regime is effective. A list of every person who used the item does not provide that technical history.

questions.prompt: Which voltage must be used when carrying out an insulation resistance test on a Class I toaster?
questions.explanation: For a conventional mains toaster that the manufacturer permits to be insulation-tested, 500 V d.c. is the standard test voltage. A lower voltage or an alternative leakage-current method is selected where electronics or surge components could be damaged.

A.text: One kilovolt is above the normal in-service setting for this straightforward mains appliance and would impose unnecessary stress. Such a voltage needs a specific product or specialist test requirement.

B.text: This resembles a production dielectric-strength level rather than a resistance-measurement voltage. Reapplying such a high AC stress routinely could damage insulation or connected components.

C.text: An insulation-resistance tester uses a defined DC output to derive the high resistance value. A mains-frequency AC stress at this magnitude is a different type of test.

D.text: For a conventional mains toaster that the manufacturer permits to be insulation-tested, 500 V d.c. is the standard test voltage. A lower voltage or an alternative leakage-current method is selected where electronics or surge components could be damaged.

questions.prompt: An insulation resistance tester should be capable of:

options.A: Delivering a maximum current of 25 A through the load
options.B: Delivering a minimum voltage of 1000 V d.c. to the load
options.C: Maintaining the test voltage required across the load
options.D: Testing the continuity of an earthing circuit

questions.explanation: An insulation-resistance tester must maintain its specified d.c. test voltage across the insulation under test so that the resistance calculation is valid. A 25 A output describes a high-current continuity method, not an insulation tester.

A.text: A current around this magnitude belongs to a selectable high-current protective-conductor bond test, not an insulation measurement. The latter uses a current-limited DC voltage across a very high resistance.

B.text: Routine equipment tests commonly select 250 V or 500 V DC according to vulnerability and manufacturer guidance. A mandatory one-kilovolt minimum would be unsuitable for many in-service products.

C.text: An insulation-resistance tester must maintain its specified d.c. test voltage across the insulation under test so that the resistance calculation is valid. A 25 A output describes a high-current continuity method, not an insulation tester.

D.text: Protective-conductor continuity is a low-resistance test with a different current characteristic. Insulation testing establishes adequate separation between parts that should not conduct.

questions.prompt: Where a user check reveals damage to equipment, it must be reported to:

options.A: A manager of an inspection and test organization

questions.explanation: A damaged item found by a user must be escalated to the responsible person. That person can arrange withdrawal, repair, replacement and recording.

A.text: An external test provider may have no control over whether the employer's item remains available for use. The workplace dutyholder needs the finding so immediate withdrawal and follow-up can be arranged.

B.text: A damaged item found by a user must be escalated to the responsible person. That person can arrange withdrawal, repair, replacement and recording.

C.text: Ordinary appliance damage is managed through the employer's safety and maintenance system, not automatically referred to the regulator. Serious incidents may create separate reporting duties, but that is not this routine case.

D.text: The maker may be consulted about instructions, warranty or a recurring design problem, but it does not control the item at the workplace. Local safety action cannot wait for that external contact.

questions.prompt: Which responsibility applies to the manager of an inspection-and-test organisation even if they do not personally operate testers or carry out repairs?

options.A: Demonstrate competence in the use of appliance testers
options.B: Instruct untrained persons in the use of portable appliance testers
options.C: Know their legal responsibilities under the Electricity at Work Regulations

questions.explanation: The manager must understand the legal responsibilities that govern the work and must arrange competent people, suitable procedures and effective control. Personally testing or repairing every item is not an inherent requirement of the management role.

A.text: A manager who personally performs tests must be competent, but management responsibility does not necessarily include operating every instrument. It does require understanding how competent people and safe systems are provided.

B.text: A brief instruction cannot replace the knowledge and training appropriate to the tests and interpretation required. The employer must ensure each person is competent for the work assigned.

C.text: The manager must understand the legal responsibilities that govern the work and must arrange competent people, suitable procedures and effective control. Personally testing or repairing every item is not an inherent requirement of the management role.

D.text: Testing management and electrical repair are different roles with different technical competence. The manager must arrange safe withdrawal and appropriate repair without personally carrying it out.

questions.prompt: Earth continuity testing may in certain circumstances be carried out by means of:

options.C: An instrument complying with BS EN 60309

questions.explanation: A low resistance ohmmeter can be used to measure the protective conductor path where appropriate. It is suited to small resistance values in continuity checks.

A.text: An audible indication shows only that some path may exist and supplies no accurate low-resistance value. It cannot assess the conductor and termination resistance against an acceptance criterion.

B.text: A low resistance ohmmeter can be used to measure the protective conductor path where appropriate. It is suited to small resistance values in continuity checks.

C.text: That designation concerns industrial plugs, socket-outlets and couplers rather than measuring instruments. Connector product compliance provides no continuity reading.

D.text: This instrument measures very high resistance between parts intended to be separated. The protective-earth path requires the opposite measurement using a suitable low-current continuity function.

questions.prompt: Which HSE guidance sets out safe construction and use of electrical test probes and leads?

options.A: BS 5490 Specification for classification of Protection
options.C: Health & Safety Executive Guidance Note GS38

questions.explanation: HSE Guidance Note GS38 explains features such as finger barriers, minimal exposed probe tips, suitable insulation, shrouded connectors and current limitation. Those controls reduce shock, arc and short-circuit risk during electrical testing.

A.text: This former enclosure-classification standard is unrelated to safe probe-tip exposure, lead insulation and protective fusing. An IP designation does not make a voltage-test lead suitable.

B.text: The installation standard requires safe verification but is not the dedicated publication on handheld probes and leads. HSE provides the specific construction and use guidance requested.

C.text: HSE Guidance Note GS38 explains features such as finger barriers, minimal exposed probe tips, suitable insulation, shrouded connectors and current limitation. Those controls reduce shock, arc and short-circuit risk during electrical testing.

D.text: This historic IEC reference concerns the effects of current on people rather than practical lead and probe design. It does not set the GS38 safeguards for routine electrical test equipment.

questions.prompt: Where protection against electric shock from equipment is provided using a protective conductor in the fixed wiring, the equipment classification would be:
questions.explanation: Protection by a protective conductor in the fixed wiring is Class I protection. The earth path allows fault current from exposed metalwork to operate the protective device.

A.text: This obsolete construction uses basic insulation without protective-earthing provision. It cannot describe an item whose fault protection expressly depends on the installation earth.

B.text: Protection by a protective conductor in the fixed wiring is Class I protection. The earth path allows fault current from exposed metalwork to operate the protective device.

C.text: This construction uses double or reinforced insulation and does not rely on protective earth for safety. It is normally identified by the double-square symbol.

D.text: This construction relies on an appropriately extra-low-voltage source rather than an installation protective conductor. Its basic shock-protection method is therefore different.

questions.prompt: A substantially continuous metal enclosure associated with Class II equipment would be classified as:
questions.explanation: A substantially continuous metal enclosure is described as metal-cased. In Class II equipment that metalwork remains unearthed but separated from live parts by suitable insulation.

A.text: An enclosure made substantially from insulating material would fit an insulation-encased description instead. The stated outer construction is conductive metal, even though safety still comes from internal insulation.

B.text: Electrical separation can be a protective measure, but this phrase is not the construction label for the described enclosure. It confuses a circuit arrangement with the material surrounding the product.

C.text: The metal is not itself an insulating medium. It remains unearthed and is made safe by basic plus supplementary, or equivalent reinforced, insulation between it and live parts.

D.text: A substantially continuous metal enclosure is described as metal-cased. In Class II equipment that metalwork remains unearthed but separated from live parts by suitable insulation.

questions.prompt: There is no provision for protective earthing or reliance upon installation conditions for which one of the following equipment?
questions.explanation: Class II equipment uses double or reinforced insulation and neither provides protective earthing nor relies on the installation for that protection. Class I and Class 0I use an earth connection in different ways, while Class III relies on a separated extra-low-voltage supply.

A.text: This obsolete class includes an earthing terminal but a supply cord without a protective conductor, so safety depends on a separate installation connection. It does not meet both conditions in the prompt.

B.text: This construction expressly relies on protective earthing of accessible conductive parts. Loss of that installation earth can leave the enclosure dangerous after an insulation fault.

C.text: Class II equipment uses double or reinforced insulation and neither provides protective earthing nor relies on the installation for that protection. Class I and Class 0I use an earth connection in different ways, while Class III relies on a separated extra-low-voltage supply.

D.text: This traditional extra-low-voltage construction does not rely on protective earth, but it does depend on an appropriately separated source. That supply condition distinguishes it from the requested definition.

questions.prompt: For conventional mains equipment that the manufacturer confirms is suitable for a standard insulation-resistance test, which test voltage is normally used?
questions.explanation: The usual test is 500 V d.c. between linked live conductors and accessible earthed parts or the appropriate enclosure. Sensitive electronics, filters and surge protection can require 250 V d.c. or a leakage-current alternative instead.

A.text: Normal mains energisation is not an insulation-resistance measurement and would operate the load rather than provide the tester's controlled DC source. Live leakage tests use different methods and precautions.

B.text: This is not the standard selectable insulation-test value used for the conventional equipment described. A reduced 250 V DC setting, rather than 230 V, may be chosen for vulnerable electronics.

C.text: The routine resistance test uses direct current, allowing the instrument to determine leakage through insulation at a defined voltage. Applying 500 V AC would be a different and more severe stress test.

D.text: The usual test is 500 V d.c. between linked live conductors and accessible earthed parts or the appropriate enclosure. Sensitive electronics, filters and surge protection can require 250 V d.c. or a leakage-current alternative instead.

questions.prompt: How should the frequency of user checks for equipment installed in industrial premises be determined?

options.D: By risk assessment using the environment, use, damage likelihood and maintenance history

questions.explanation: Industrial conditions can justify frequent checks, but 'weekly' is not a universal legal interval. The dutyholder sets and reviews the frequency from the equipment's environment, use, likelihood of damage and defects previously found.

A.text: A pre-use check may be justified where damage can occur between uses, but it is not automatically necessary for every item described by an old movement category. Actual exposure and consequences must drive the interval.

B.text: Daily examination can suit harsh or heavily abused equipment, yet industrial premises vary greatly. Applying that calendar period universally ignores condition, users, installation and previous findings.

C.text: A monthly plan may prove reasonable for a particular asset but cannot be selected from the workplace label alone. The dutyholder must justify it and revise it as evidence accumulates.

D.text: Industrial conditions can justify frequent checks, but 'weekly' is not a universal legal interval. The dutyholder sets and reviews the frequency from the equipment's environment, use, likelihood of damage and defects previously found.

questions.prompt: During a formal visual inspection it should be confirmed that the equipment is being operated:
questions.explanation: Formal visual inspection includes confirming the appliance is used as the maker intended. Manufacturer's instructions define correct loading, environment, ventilation and operation.

A.text: Supply compatibility is important but addresses only one aspect of safe use. The maker may also specify environment, ventilation, accessories, loading, duty cycle and operating precautions.

B.text: Many ordinary products are designed for general users and do not require electrical skill. Any higher competence requirement must come from the task, risk assessment and maker information.

C.text: Specific instruction can be necessary for some work equipment, but it is not universal. The broader inspection criterion is compliance with all relevant operating information supplied for that item.
