D.text: Formal visual inspection includes confirming the appliance is used as the maker intended. Manufacturer's instructions define correct loading, environment, ventilation and operation.

questions.prompt: If a standard 13 A plug became overheated the most likely cause would be:

options.A: A loose connection at one or more of the terminals
options.C: Reversed polarity of the cable conductors
options.D: The use of an incorrectly rated cartridge fuse

questions.explanation: A loose plug terminal creates resistance at the connection. Load current through that resistance produces heat, making it the most likely cause of overheating.

A.text: A loose plug terminal creates resistance at the connection. Load current through that resistance produces heat, making it the most likely cause of overheating.

B.text: A poor protective-earth path is a serious shock-protection defect, but under normal load it carries no operating current. It therefore does not usually create the localized heating seen at line or neutral terminals.

C.text: Incorrect line and neutral assignment creates isolation and shock hazards but does not by itself increase normal load current or terminal resistance. It is not the usual thermal mechanism.

D.text: An oversized fuse can fail to protect a flex during overload, so its rating must be corrected. Without an overload, however, it is less direct than a resistive terminal joint as the source of plug heating.

questions.prompt: Using the conventional IET in-service criterion, what is the usual minimum insulation resistance for Class I equipment other than heating equipment above 3 kW?
questions.explanation: The usual Class I minimum is 1 MΩ. Heating equipment above 3 kW has historically used a different 0.3 MΩ criterion; manufacturer information and equipment construction still determine whether an insulation-resistance test is appropriate.

A.text: Half a megohm is below the ordinary Class I acceptance value and should trigger investigation of the test setup, connected components and insulation condition. It is not the large-heater exception either.

B.text: The usual Class I minimum is 1 MΩ. Heating equipment above 3 kW has historically used a different 0.3 MΩ criterion; manufacturer information and equipment construction still determine whether an insulation-resistance test is appropriate.

C.text: This is the usual minimum associated with Class II equipment, which relies wholly on double or reinforced insulation. A Class I item may exceed it, but it is not the threshold requested.

D.text: Seven megohms would be a healthy result for many products but is not the published minimum boundary. Confusing a desirable high reading with the pass limit would reject serviceable equipment unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: An ohmmeter used to measure the resistance of an earth-continuity conductor must be capable of producing a short-circuit current between:
questions.explanation: A suitable low-resistance ohmmeter uses a test current in the 20-200 mA range for this low-current protective-conductor continuity method. It provides a stable, useful reading without the stress of a high-current bond test.

A.text: This very small signal range falls below the low-current protective-conductor method specified for PAT instruments. It may not provide the intended measurement performance at joints and contacts.

B.text: A suitable low-resistance ohmmeter uses a test current in the 20-200 mA range for this low-current protective-conductor continuity method. It provides a stable, useful reading without the stress of a high-current bond test.

C.text: The lower boundary touches the top of the stated low-current range, but the upper value exceeds it. A higher-current bond test is a separate selectable method with different equipment considerations.

D.text: This stops at the lower boundary rather than spanning the recognized low-current continuity range. The selected instrument should be capable throughout the specified band up to 200 mA.

questions.prompt: When no product-specific value is given, what maximum protective-conductor or touch current is commonly used for portable or hand-held Class I equipment?
questions.explanation: The commonly used limit is 0.75 mA for portable or hand-held Class I equipment. This is a current measured by a leakage method, not an insulation-resistance reading, so the original question incorrectly mixed two different tests.

A.text: This is the commonly stated touch-current limit for Class II equipment, which has no protective-earth conductor. It is not the general value for the earthed portable category described.

B.text: Half a milliampere is associated with other extra-low-voltage or historical categories rather than this Class I limit. It is below, but does not define, the requested maximum.

C.text: The commonly used limit is 0.75 mA for portable or hand-held Class I equipment. This is a current measured by a leakage method, not an insulation-resistance reading, so the original question incorrectly mixed two different tests.

D.text: One milliampere exceeds the commonly applied limit for a portable or hand-held earthed product. It should not be confused with the one-megohm insulation-resistance threshold.

questions.prompt: Which option provides all three practical controls used by this equipment-maintenance scheme when an item is found faulty?

options.A: Label and report it while leaving it available
options.B: Label and withdraw it without reporting the defect
options.C: Identify it as faulty, report it and withdraw it from service
options.D: Report it while leaving it available

questions.explanation: The item must be taken out of use and the fault reported so repair or replacement can be controlled. Clearly identifying it as faulty helps stop someone else putting it back into service before that action is complete.

A.text: A warning can be overlooked or removed, so the dangerous item remains capable of being used. Physical or administrative withdrawal is needed until competent repair or replacement.

B.text: Removal controls the immediate exposure, but silence prevents the responsible person from arranging corrective action and updating the maintenance system. The defect must enter the management process.

C.text: The item must be taken out of use and the fault reported so repair or replacement can be controlled. Clearly identifying it as faulty helps stop someone else putting it back into service before that action is complete.

D.text: Notification alone does not prevent another worker from energising the item before action is taken. The equipment must be made unavailable as soon as the unsafe condition is identified.

questions.prompt: If sensitive electronic equipment could be damaged by an applied-voltage insulation-resistance test, which alternative can assess its leakage under suitable operating conditions?
questions.explanation: A suitable protective-conductor or touch-current test measures leakage without applying the 500 V d.c. insulation test that may stress filters, surge devices or electronics. The tester must select the method and limits for the equipment's class and manufacturer guidance.

A.text: This can verify a protective-conductor path but does not assess unwanted current from live circuits to earth or accessible parts. It answers a different safety question.

B.text: This method applies an even greater electrical stress than routine insulation resistance and is more likely to harm vulnerable components. It is not a protective alternative for sensitive electronics.

C.text: Correct conductor assignment matters for leads and controls, but it supplies no leakage-current measurement. A product can have correct polarity while its insulation or filters produce an unsafe current.

D.text: A suitable protective-conductor or touch-current test measures leakage without applying the 500 V d.c. insulation test that may stress filters, surge devices or electronics. The tester must select the method and limits for the equipment's class and manufacturer guidance.

questions.prompt: Which supply arrangement is commonly required where equipment is designed for protective-conductor current above 3.5 mA but not exceeding 10 mA?

options.A: Be permanently wired or supplied through an appropriate BS EN 60309-2 plug and socket
options.B: Have a label permanently fixed indicating the value of leakage current
options.C: Have internal protective conductors of not less than 0.5 mm² c.s.a
options.D: Only be used in industrial situations

questions.explanation: Above 3.5 mA, a casual domestic plug connection may not give the required reliability of protective earthing. Permanent connection or an appropriate industrial plug-and-socket arrangement provides a more dependable earth path; still higher currents can require additional measures.

A.text: Above 3.5 mA, a casual domestic plug connection may not give the required reliability of protective earthing. Permanent connection or an appropriate industrial plug-and-socket arrangement provides a more dependable earth path; still higher currents can require additional measures.

B.text: A warning can communicate the high-current condition but does not make the earth connection mechanically secure. Labelling cannot replace the required supply arrangement.

C.text: This conductor size is not the connection control specified for the stated current range and may be inadequate for the product. External protective-path reliability remains essential.

D.text: Workplace type does not remove the shock hazard created if the protective connection is lost. The equipment needs the prescribed connection wherever it is installed.

questions.prompt: In order to reduce the possibility of electric shock through contact with live parts, the aperture of any electrical equipment must

options.A: Be located so as to be inaccessible to the user
options.B: Be subjected to dielectric strength testing
options.C: Comply with the requirements of BS EN 50950
options.D: Meet test finger and test pin requirements

questions.explanation: Apertures must prevent access to live parts by standard test fingers and pins. Passing those tests shows the enclosure gives effective basic protection.

A.text: Normal placement can change during installation, servicing or misuse and does not prove the enclosure prevents access. The opening itself must provide the required basic protection.

B.text: A high-voltage test assesses insulation strength rather than whether a finger or small object can reach a live part. An enclosure can pass one property while failing the other.

C.text: This obsolete and incorrectly cited product-standard reference cannot serve as a universal aperture criterion. Equipment must meet the applicable current product standard and access-probe requirements.

D.text: Apertures must prevent access to live parts by standard test fingers and pins. Passing those tests shows the enclosure gives effective basic protection.

questions.prompt: For protection against electric shock, Class III equipment relies upon a supply derived from a
questions.explanation: Class III equipment relies on SELV for shock protection. The supply must be separated from higher-voltage circuits so dangerous voltage cannot appear at the equipment.

A.text: FELV uses extra-low voltage for function but does not necessarily provide the separation and protective conditions needed for shock protection. Additional protective measures can therefore be required.

B.text: PELV may have an intentional connection to earth and is a distinct installation measure. The traditional Class III definition is associated with the separated arrangement.

C.text: This wording is not the formal expansion of SELV in current BS 7671 terminology. The essential feature is electrical separation from higher-voltage systems and earth, not the informal word safety alone.

D.text: Class III equipment relies on SELV for shock protection. The supply must be separated from higher-voltage circuits so dangerous voltage cannot appear at the equipment.

questions.prompt: In the traditional protective-class model, which arrangement describes ordinary metal-cased Class II equipment where no functional-earth facility is provided?

options.A: Protectively earthed metalwork separated from live parts by basic and supplementary insulation
options.B: Earthed metalwork separated from live parts by basic insulation only
options.C: Unearthed metalwork separated from live parts by basic and supplementary insulation
options.D: Unearthed metalwork separated from live parts by basic insulation only

questions.explanation: Ordinary metal-cased Class II equipment does not use protective earthing. Its accessible metal enclosure is kept unearthed and separated from live parts by double insulation, represented here by basic plus supplementary insulation.

A.text: Protective earthing of accessible metal is not the defining arrangement for Class II construction. Its safety must not depend on an installation protective conductor, even where a separate functional-earth facility exists.

B.text: Basic insulation plus protective earthing describes the two principal layers of Class I fault protection. It does not provide the earth-independent double-insulation construction requested.

C.text: Ordinary metal-cased Class II equipment does not use protective earthing. Its accessible metal enclosure is kept unearthed and separated from live parts by double insulation, represented here by basic plus supplementary insulation.

D.text: A single layer can leave accessible metal hazardous after one insulation fault. Supplementary or equivalent reinforced insulation is required where protective earth is not the safety measure.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following types of equipment in shops and offices is considered the most likely to develop dangerous faults?
questions.explanation: Hand-held equipment is continually gripped and moved, and its flexible lead, strain relief and enclosure receive more mechanical stress. That makes damage capable of exposing live parts more likely than with equipment left stationary.

A.text: Hand-held equipment is continually gripped and moved, and its flexible lead, strain relief and enclosure receive more mechanical stress. That makes damage capable of exposing live parts more likely than with equipment left stationary.

B.text: An item that can be relocated may still spend most of its energized life resting in one position. It usually experiences less continuous flexing and direct body contact than equipment gripped during operation.

C.text: Readily carried equipment can be exposed to handling damage, but it is not necessarily held throughout use. The more direct category in the question combines continuous handling, flex movement and close user contact.

D.text: Equipment normally remaining in one place is generally exposed to less mechanical movement of its case and supply lead. Its risk can still be high for other environmental or operational reasons.

questions.prompt: When formally inspecting equipment used outdoors, which rating helps confirm that its enclosure suits the expected dust and water exposure?
questions.explanation: The IP rating describes protection against entry of solid objects and water. The required digits depend on the actual outdoor conditions; the letters GP, GS and IT do not provide an enclosure-ingress classification.

A.text: This is not the standardized enclosure code for entry of solids and water. An invented abbreviation gives no verifiable evidence that outdoor exposure has been considered.

B.text: GS is associated with HSE guidance identifiers such as GS38, not an ingress-protection classification on equipment. It does not state resistance to rain, dust or object access.

C.text: The IP rating describes protection against entry of solid objects and water. The required digits depend on the actual outdoor conditions; the letters GP, GS and IT do not provide an enclosure-ingress classification.

D.text: IT commonly refers to information technology or an earthing-system designation, neither of which specifies enclosure protection. Outdoor suitability needs the recognized two-character ingress code.

questions.prompt: If an inspector considers that the equipment being tested is not suitable for the environment, this should be

options.A: Recorded after the operative has been instructed as to the possible danger
options.B: Recorded and brought to the attention of the responsible person
options.C: Reported to the Health & Safety Executive
options.D: Reported to the manufacturer of the equipment

questions.explanation: Unsuitability for the environment is a safety finding that must be recorded. It also needs to be brought to the responsible person's attention so corrective action can be taken.

A.text: Warning only the immediate user does not ensure the dutyholder can remove, relocate or replace the unsuitable item. The finding needs management attention and an auditable outcome.

B.text: Unsuitability for the environment is a safety finding that must be recorded. It also needs to be brought to the responsible person's attention so corrective action can be taken.

C.text: Routine unsuitability is normally managed by the employer or person controlling the equipment. Regulatory reporting may arise after specified serious incidents, not for every maintenance observation.

D.text: The maker may clarify environmental ratings, but the workplace controller must act on the present risk. An external enquiry does not itself prevent continued use in the wrong conditions.

questions.prompt: For simple mains equipment that the manufacturer permits to be insulation-tested, which preparation includes its internal circuits while keeping the enclosure safe?

options.A: Fuses should be checked, switches in the OFF position and all covers removed if possible
options.B: Fuses should be checked, switches in the ON position and covers in place
options.C: Switches should be in the OFF position and all covers in place
options.D: Switches should be in the ON position and all covers removed if possible

questions.explanation: With the item isolated from the mains, serviceable fuses and switches in the ON position let the test reach its internal circuits. Covers remain in place for safety; electronic controls may need a different manufacturer-approved preparation or test.

A.text: An open control can exclude internal wiring from the measurement, while removing covers creates needless access to parts. The equipment should remain assembled in its safe-use condition.

B.text: With the item isolated from the mains, serviceable fuses and switches in the ON position let the test reach its internal circuits. Covers remain in place for safety; electronic controls may need a different manufacturer-approved preparation or test.

C.text: Keeping covers fitted is appropriate, but an open switch can leave conductors and components beyond it outside the test path. The selected method must include all relevant live circuitry.

D.text: Closing the controls helps include internal paths, but enclosure removal is unnecessary and may expose or disturb parts. Testing should be performed with normal protective covers secured.

questions.prompt: When conducting an earth continuity test on equipment that has accessible metal parts, which are earthed only for functional/screening purposes, these parts should be

options.A: Subjected to a measured touch current test
options.B: Tested at a current 1.5 times the fuse rating
options.C: Tested at a current between 20 mA and 200 mA
options.D: Tested for earth continuity at full current

questions.explanation: A low-current 20-200 mA continuity test can confirm the functional or screening connection without forcing a high bond current through a path that was not designed as the appliance's protective-earth route.

A.text: A touch-current assessment may be separately appropriate, but it does not answer how to verify the stated functional-earth path. The question specifically asks for the continuity-test treatment.

B.text: That historical high-current bond method can overstress a screening connection not intended for protective fault current. A low-current measurement is the suitable continuity approach here.

C.text: A low-current 20-200 mA continuity test can confirm the functional or screening connection without forcing a high bond current through a path that was not designed as the appliance's protective-earth route.

D.text: Applying an unspecified maximum output risks damage to delicate tracks, screens or components. Test current should be deliberately limited while still providing a reliable low-resistance reading.

questions.prompt: When using certain types of test instrument, as an alternative to subtracting the lead resistance from the final measured value, the lead resistance may be
questions.explanation: Nulling compensates for the resistance of the test leads before measuring the appliance. It avoids having to subtract the lead resistance manually from the final reading.

A.text: The physical resistance of the leads is not deliberately reduced by an instrument setting. Compensation stores an offset so that their contribution is removed from subsequent displayed results.

B.text: Lead resistance can be significant beside a protective-conductor acceptance value and would make the equipment appear worse than it is. It must be measured and compensated, not simply disregarded.

C.text: Adding further resistance would enlarge the measurement error and make comparison with the limit less reliable. The aim is to remove the known lead contribution from the displayed value.

D.text: Nulling compensates for the resistance of the test leads before measuring the appliance. It avoids having to subtract the lead resistance manually from the final reading.

questions.prompt: An insulation-resistance test between linked live conductors and earth on Class I equipment gives only 0.1 MΩ. What fault could cause this low reading?

options.A: A short circuit between live conductors within the appliance cord set
options.B: An open circuit has occurred within the protective conductor
options.C: Progressive failure of the insulation between live conductors
options.D: Progressive failure of the insulation between live conductors and earth

questions.explanation: Only 0.1 MΩ between linked live conductors and earth indicates a substantial leakage path through deteriorating live-to-earth insulation. A live-to-live fault or an open protective conductor would not by itself create that measured path to earth.

A.text: Line and neutral are intentionally linked together for this measurement, so a connection between them does not create the observed path to earth. It is dangerous for other reasons but not this result mechanism.

B.text: A broken earth is detected by protective-conductor continuity and may even remove part of the reference path. It does not create the substantial leakage needed to produce a very low live-to-earth resistance.

C.text: Deterioration only between line and neutral lies within the linked side of this test and is not measured as leakage to the enclosure. A separate fault path to earth is needed to depress this reading.

D.text: Only 0.1 MΩ between linked live conductors and earth indicates a substantial leakage path through deteriorating live-to-earth insulation. A live-to-live fault or an open protective conductor would not by itself create that measured path to earth.

questions.prompt: In the traditional equipment-class system, which class relies on supply at separated extra-low voltage and does not rely on protective earthing?
questions.explanation: Traditional Class III equipment is supplied at separated extra-low voltage and does not rely on a protective-earth connection. Some modern product standards use energy-source classes instead, so the traditional-class qualification is important.

A.text: Class 0 uses basic insulation alone and has no protective-earth connection. Its absence of an earth does not mean that its protection is provided by an extra-low-voltage supply.

B.text: Class I combines basic insulation with protective earthing of accessible conductive parts, so it does rely on an earth connection rather than SELV alone.

C.text: Class II obtains shock protection from double or reinforced insulation. Its defining measure is enhanced insulation, not operation from a separated extra-low-voltage source.

D.text: Traditional Class III equipment is supplied at separated extra-low voltage and does not rely on a protective-earth connection. Some modern product standards use energy-source classes instead, so the traditional-class qualification is important.

questions.prompt: On what date did the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 generally come into force?
questions.explanation: Although their title and statutory-instrument number use 1989, regulation 1 states that the Electricity at Work Regulations came into force on 1 April 1990.

A.text: The year 1989 appears in the Regulations' title and statutory-instrument number, but regulation 1 set their commencement for the following year.

B.text: Although their title and statutory-instrument number use 1989, regulation 1 states that the Electricity at Work Regulations came into force on 1 April 1990.

C.text: The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations date from 1999; that year is not the commencement year of the Electricity at Work Regulations.

D.text: By 2004 the Electricity at Work Regulations had already been in force for fourteen years, so this date is much too late.

questions.prompt: The most important check on a portable appliance is:
questions.explanation: Visual inspection is the most important PAT check because it finds common hazards before instruments are used. Damaged plugs, leads, cases and signs of overheating are often visible.

A.text: Reviewing inspection information does not examine the appliance's present condition, so damage that occurred since the review may be missed.

B.text: Production testing checks equipment during manufacture; it does not assess deterioration, damage or misuse after the appliance enters service.

C.text: Type testing validates a representative design or sample. It does not establish the current condition of each appliance in service.

D.text: Visual inspection is the most important PAT check because it finds common hazards before instruments are used. Damaged plugs, leads, cases and signs of overheating are often visible.

questions.prompt: Under current IET guidance, how should the initial combined inspection-and-testing interval for Class I IT equipment in a school be set?

options.A: By the dutyholder from a risk assessment and previous maintenance findings
options.B: Exactly every 24 months in every school
options.C: Exactly every 3 months in every school
options.D: Exactly every 6 months in every school

questions.explanation: The current IET Code removed the old fixed-frequency table. The dutyholder selects and reviews an interval using the environment, users, equipment construction and use, installation method, manufacturer information and previous findings.

A.text: The current IET Code removed the old fixed-frequency table. The dutyholder selects and reviews an interval using the environment, users, equipment construction and use, installation method, manufacturer information and previous findings.

B.text: A two-year interval may suit some low-risk equipment, but the current Code does not prescribe it for every school regardless of use, location or defect history.

C.text: Three-monthly combined testing would be unnecessarily frequent for much protected IT equipment and cannot be imposed without considering the actual risk.

D.text: Six months is another fixed calendar answer that ignores whether the equipment is static, heavily handled, damaged frequently or used in a harsh area.

questions.prompt: Under current IET guidance, which earth-continuity approach is generally preferred for routine in-service testing?

options.A: A mandatory 10 A test for every item
options.B: A mandatory 15 A test for every item
options.C: A suitable lower-current continuity test selected for the equipment
options.D: A mandatory 35 A test for every item

questions.explanation: The 5th edition gives preference to a suitable lower-current earth-continuity test. A high-current test up to 25 A remains available on some instruments, but it is not a universal instrument requirement or routine default.

A.text: Ten amperes is available on some testers or in some national modes, but current IET guidance does not make it compulsory for every construction.

B.text: A universal 15 A rule has no basis in the current risk- and equipment-based selection of earth-continuity methods.

C.text: The 5th edition gives preference to a suitable lower-current earth-continuity test. A high-current test up to 25 A remains available on some instruments, but it is not a universal instrument requirement or routine default.

D.text: Thirty-five amperes is above the traditional high-current PAT value of about 25 A and could apply needless stress without improving a routine measurement.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a PAT tester's 'soft' earth-continuity test?

options.A: A high-current test applied for a shorter time
options.C: An insulation test at a reduced voltage
options.D: A functional test below normal supply voltage

questions.explanation: 'Soft' describes the lower-current earth-continuity method used to measure the protective path without applying an unnecessarily high bond current. It is not an insulation or functional test.

A.text: The traditional high-current bond measurement is described as the hard test. Short duration does not turn that high-current method into a soft test.

B.text: 'Soft' describes the lower-current earth-continuity method used to measure the protective path without applying an unnecessarily high bond current. It is not an insulation or functional test.

C.text: An insulation test measures resistance between live conductors and accessible or earthed parts. It does not measure continuity of the protective conductor.

D.text: A functional check confirms that equipment operates as intended. It is separate from measuring the resistance of its protective-earth path.

questions.prompt: When assessing earth continuity of an extension lead, which limit accounts for the lead conductor's length and cross-sectional area?

options.A: 0.1 Ω plus the calculated protective-conductor resistance R
options.B: 0.1 Ω regardless of the lead length
options.C: Any resistance is acceptable if the lead is shorter than 15 m
options.D: The RCD rating alone determines the continuity limit

questions.explanation: The continuity limit includes the resistance of the lead's protective conductor: 0.1 Ω + R. R is calculated from conductor material, cross-sectional area and length, so a single 15 m boundary is not the complete current pass criterion.

A.text: The continuity limit includes the resistance of the lead's protective conductor: 0.1 Ω + R. R is calculated from conductor material, cross-sectional area and length, so a single 15 m boundary is not the complete current pass criterion.

B.text: A longer or smaller protective conductor has more inherent resistance. Applying 0.1 Ω alone can reject a sound long lead or fail to distinguish its expected cord resistance.

C.text: A short lead can still contain a broken, loose or corroded protective conductor. Its measured result must remain within the calculated continuity limit.

D.text: An RCD's residual operating current does not calculate the resistance of the lead's earth core. The conductor material, area and length determine R.

questions.prompt: Formal visual inspections should be carried out by:
questions.explanation: A formal visual inspection requires competence because it involves judgement and may include checks users should not attempt. User checks are simpler and limited to obvious defects.

A.text: Users can be trained to make simple pre-use checks, but a formal inspection requires additional knowledge and judgement beyond the ordinary user role.

B.text: Including people who are not competent defeats the control. Anyone assigned the formal inspection must have suitable training, skills and knowledge for that task.

C.text: A formal visual inspection requires competence because it involves judgement and may include checks users should not attempt. User checks are simpler and limited to obvious defects.

D.text: A manufacturer may provide useful instructions, but its representative is not required to perform every formal inspection; competence is the deciding requirement.

questions.prompt: After safely isolating permanently connected equipment at a flex outlet, which listed instrument can perform dead insulation-resistance and continuity measurements?

options.B: A dedicated portable appliance test instrument

questions.explanation: An insulation/continuity tester can perform the relevant dead measurements once the equipment is safely isolated and the test method is suitable for its construction. A plug-in PAT sequence cannot simply be assumed for permanently connected equipment.

A.text: A clamp ammeter measures current in an energised conductor without opening the circuit. It does not perform dead insulation-resistance or low-resistance continuity tests.

B.text: A standard PAT sequence expects plug-connected equipment. Permanently connected equipment needs a method and connections suited to the isolated flex outlet rather than an assumed plug-in routine.
